results.notes: Bulk chemistry and mineral percentages in the db match the Dec 2025 SRT datasheet exactly (oxide total 99.15 incl. LOI; db oxide_sum 98.74 is the same list excluding LOI). The failure is entirely in the physical properties: all four geotechnical/physical numbers stored for LHS-1 are verbatim the LHS-1D dust-grade values (0.81 / 10.22 / 0.205 / 28.62), i.e. numbers were transferred between product variants. The correct LHS-1 values are 1.40 g/cm3, 81.62 um, 0.311 kPa, 31.49 deg. The datasheet also states Angle of Repose (10g) 22.62 deg and (250g) 36.58 deg, which have no field in this schema. specific_gravity 2.77 is unsupported: I checked the Dec 2025, Dec 2023 (003-01-001-1223) and 2021 (001-01-001-0120) LHS-1 revisions and none states a specific gravity. Page 2 of the datasheet is only a particle-size-distribution curve - no extra numbers, no glass content %, no NASA figure-of-merit. Note also that the db tags R084 (Yin & Cheng, Planet. Space Sci.) as the 'composition' reference; the manufacturer datasheet, not that paper, is the composition source. For context, the older Jan 2020 revision (001-01-001-0120) carries a completely different, superseded chemistry (SiO2 48.1, Al2O3 25.8, CaO 18.4, Fe2O3 3.7, ... Total 99.9) - do not mix it with the current values.

Importantly the DB correctly carries FeO 3.6 as FeO (not converted to Fe2O3), matching the sheet. Bulk density 1.3 and D50 42 um match. The DB mineral_sum 99.98 is the correct arithmetic sum of the six listed components; the sheet does not print a mineralogy total. The sheet's printed oxide Total 99.5 matches the DB oxide_sum 99.54 within rounding. The fact sheet carries a SECOND, separate table headed 'Agglutinate Mineralogy' (Anorthosite 99.0, Iron Powder 1.0) which describes the composition of the agglutinate component alone, not the bulk simulant - I deliberately did not merge it into the mineral list, as doing so would double-count. Source data also states, and the DB omits: Mean Particle Size 93 um (the schema has no mean-size field) and Angle of Repose (10 g) 44.4 deg, (250 g) 42.78 deg. results.notes: Manufacturer fact sheet held locally; I also opened all four older revisions in SRT/older/ (001-02-001-0120 2021, 002-02-001-0621 Dec2022, 003-02-001-1223 Dec2023, 003-02-001-0525 Jun2025) to check whether the db numbers came from a superseded sheet. They did not: 2021 gives SiO2 40.2 / Fe2O3 13.9 / TiO2 7.3, Dec2022 gives SiO2 46.9 / TiO2 3.6, and Dec2023 and Jun2025 both give exactly the same chemistry as Dec2025 (48.22 / 2.70 / 12.40 / 8.79 / 0.06 / 15.97 / 7.65 / 1.73 / 0.42 / 0.23 / 0.56, Total 98.87). results.name: DUST-Y
results.source_title: Lunar Simulant Assessment - Denevi, B.W. (POC), Blewett, D.T., Cahill, J.T.S., Greenhagen, B.T., Hibbitts, K., Hurley, D.M., Klima, R.L., Martin, A.C., Montalbano, T.J., Patterson, G.W., Stickle, A.M., Stockstill-Cahill, K., Wagoner, C.M.; Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, 30 January 2020 (LSIC Lunar Simulants Working Group)
results.evidence_quote:
Exolith also produces a dust simulant (DUST-Y) with a mean particle size of ~8 µm. Currently,
this dust simulant is simply the fines created as a by-product during the grinding of materials for
other simulants, with limited control on composition; however, if there is a desire for a dust
simulant with compositional fidelity, that could be created.

No nanophase iron is included in any of their simulants. Exolith does not produce synthetic
agglutinates.
db_discrepancies: minerals_in_db 'Ilmenite': DB 0.1%; source publishes no mineralogy for DUST-Y and states its composition is not controlled.
minerals_in_db 'Olivine': DB 0.2%; source publishes no mineralogy for DUST-Y.
minerals_in_db 'Pyroxene': DB 0.4%; source publishes no mineralogy for DUST-Y.
minerals_in_db 'Glass': DB 9.0%; source publishes no mineralogy for DUST-Y.
mineral_sum: DB 9.7; source publishes no mineralogy. A mineral assemblage summing to 9.7% is not a composition under any reading, and the DB's own scorecard already flags it as 'outside 90-101%'.

institution: DB 'Space Resource Technologies'; the source attributes DUST-Y to Exolith (CLASS Exolith Lab, University of Central Florida). DUST-Y does not appear anywhere in the current Space Resource Technologies simulant catalogue.
type: DB 'Highlands'; the source says DUST-Y is the fines by-product of grinding materials for other simulants, so it has no highlands (or mare) designation.

references_in_db: DB cites R016, Duri et al. (2022) 'The potential for lunar and martian regolith simulants to sustain plant growth: A multidisciplinary overview' - a review/overview paper, which under the source quality order is review_or_secondary and is not an acceptable composition source; and extra_reference cites Britt & Cannon (2019) 'Mineralogically Accurate Simulants for Lunar ISRU', which is about the mineralogically-designed LHS/LMS product line, not about DUST-Y.
results.notes: I located the defining description of DUST-Y and it explicitly states the product has no controlled composition, so no composition can be reported for it. What I actually opened and read: (1) the JHU APL / LSIC 'Lunar Simulant Assessment' (30 Jan 2020), downloaded and saved to the papers directory, extracted with pdftotext -layout; DUST-Y appears exactly once in all 28 pages, at the quoted passage, and is absent from the report's own section 3.5 'Composition'; (2) the Space Resource Technologies full simulant catalogue at spaceresourcetech.com/collections/all-simulants, which lists 21 products and contains no DUST-Y - the only dust grades sold are LHS-1D (Lunar Highlands Dust) and LMS-1D (Lunar Mare Dust), and per the ground rules I did NOT transfer either of their compositions onto DUST-Y; (3) the producer's own conference abstract, Landsman & Britt, 'Simulated Asteroid and Planetary Materials at the CLASS Exolith Lab', EPSC2020-906, whose entire DUST-Y entry reads 'DUST-Y: Physical silicate dust simulant with ~1-10 micron particles. Useful for fine dust mitigation studies.' - particle size only, no oxides and no mineralogy. So no manufacturer datasheet exists for this product and no primary characterisation paper publishes a composition for it. The only quantitative property any source states is a mean particle size of ~8 µm (LSIC 2020) / ~1-10 µm particles (EPSC2020-906); I left the physical block empty rather than write ~8 µm into particle_size_d50, because a mean is not a D50 and the sources state no D50. Recommendation for the database: delete the four mineral entries entirely - they are unsourced, they sum to 9.7%, and they cannot be repaired because the defining source says the material's composition is deliberately uncontrolled. Record DUST-Y as a particle-size-defined dust with composition 'not specified by producer'.

problems: APL/LSIC Lunar Simulant Assessment (30 Jan 2020) p.6: DUST-Y is 'simply the fines created as a by-product during the grinding of materials for other simulants, with limited control on composition' — confirmed in the saved PDF

All 13 oxide values and all 11 mineral/amorphous values in the DB match Table 1 and Table 2 of TDS-TLM-0-v1.1 exactly. Recomputed sums: oxides 98.61, minerals 100.0 — identical to the DB's stored sums. Physical measurements match: mean density 1.52 g/cm3, PSD median 48.4 um, cohesion 13.299 kPa, friction angle 34.617 deg, glass 31.4 %, mean NASA FoM 81.8 %. The verdict is DB_WRONG_SOURCE_FOUND on the strength of one genuine numeric error: physical.ti_content_percent = 0.82 while this product's TiO2 is 1.72 wt% — 0.82 is TLH-0's (S065) value, i.e. a cross-variant carry-over, which also contradicts the DB's own oxide row TiO2 = 1.72 for S066. The most likely explanation is that APL characterised a titanium-enhanced batch: datasheet footnote [1] says 'The titanium component can be increased with an ilmenite additive upon request', and OPR sells that as a separate product, OPRL2NT (10% anorthosite / 75.6% basaltic cinder / 14.4% ilmenite, per offplanetresearch.com/products-and-services). results.notes: All eight db oxides match NASA/TM-20240011783 Rev A Table 7 exactly, and db particle_size_d50 46.9 matches its Table 10 Q50 exactly, so the composition on record is sourced, not fabricated. TWO CAVEATS THE CURATOR MUST SEE. (1) PROVENANCE: Table 7 attributes the OPRH4W30 row to 'OPR Datasheet', but 48.1/0.2/30.3/1.7/1.1/15.2/2.3/0.1 is exactly the OPRH4N column of the OPR General Lunar Regolith Simulants Data Sheet (48.07/0.20/30.28/1.69/1.08/15.23/2.29/0.10) rounded to one decimal. OPRH4W30 is OPRH4N plus 30% agglutinates; agglutinates are glass-rich and would be expected to shift the bulk chemistry, so these look like OPRH4N numbers carried over rather than an independent analysis of OPRH4W30. The 2024 OPR datasheet on disk does not list OPRH4W30 at all and states 'The information in this document should only be used for the listed general simulants.' I recommend the db entry keep these values but carry an explicit caveat, or that OPR be asked directly. (2) NO MANUFACTURER DATASHEET EXISTS PUBLICLY for OPRH4W30: I checked offplanetresearch.com/products-and-services (lists OPRH2N/H3N/H4N/L2N/L2NT/FLCROSS2 and 'custom agglutinates', no OPRH4W30 and no PDF links), and searched for the 2025 OPR datasheet revision cited as ref [4] of the LPSC abstract - not publicly retrievable. So the agency report is the best obtainable source. (3) The db oxide_sum is 99.0 and the guide publishes no total, so that sum is a computed field, which is fine. (4) The db minerals list is empty; Table 5 gives Agglutinates 30 / Anorthosite 90 / Basalt 10 for OPRH4W30, which is a feedstock recipe (it sums to 130, i.e. 30 parts agglutinate added to a 90/10 anorthosite-basalt base), NOT modal mineralogy - the guide's own Table 4 scores OPRH4W30 mineralogy as 'n/a' for insufficient data. Do not present those three numbers as a mineral mode. (5) Additional sourced OPRH4W30 data I read: NASA/TM-20240011783 Table 13 particle shape AR 0.61, sqrt(FF) 0.90 (SDL 2022 JSC-ARES); crystalline silica table, total crystalline silica 1.60 wt%, respirable (<10 um) fraction 16.3%, total respirable crystalline silica 0.26 wt% (2023 analysis) and 1.73 wt% total (2021); Roth, Roux & Roux 2025 LPSC #2695 static angle of repose 42.1 +/- 1.6 deg, and its Table 1 note '*The agglutinates in OPRH4W30 are made from the same base composition as OPRH4N.'

problems: NASA/TM-20240011783 Rev A Table 7 row confirmed (48.1/0.2/30.3/1.7/1.1/15.2/2.3/0.1, 'OPR Datasheet'); Roth, Roux & Roux 2025 LPSC 2695 state the OPRH4W30 agglutinates share OPRH4N's base composition, so this chemistry is the base blend, not a measurement of the finished product. Minerals row '30 / 90 / 10' is 30 % agglutinates added to a 90/10 base, not a modal analysis.

db_discrepancies: minerals_in_db 'Magnetite' pct: db 0.7 vs source: no source I opened reports magnetite in any NU-LHT product. The only 'Magnetite' figure anywhere in the NU-LHT literature I read is Stoeser TM-2010-216438 Table 5, 'MT (Magnetite) 2.42 Wt%', which is the CIPW norm of the Stillwater mill-sand FEEDSTOCK, not a simulant. The nearest 0.7-ish number is 'Ilmenite 0.73' in the ARES 'NU-LHT-1M Prototype' column — a different mineral and a different material.

minerals_in_db 'Glass' pct: db 19.7 vs source: no source states 19.7% glass for 'NU-LHT'. 19.7 appears only in the ARES 'Modal Mineralogy' column headed 'NU-LHT-1M Prototype (%)', i.e. a specific 1M prototype batch, not the family.
mineral_sum: db 20.4 vs source: no source; a two-mineral list summing to 20.4% is not a composition.

physical.glass_content_percent: db 40.0 vs source: no source states 40% glass for any NU-LHT product. 40% glass is the specification of NUW-LHT-5M only (NASA/TM-20240011783 Rev A p.22: 'The crystalline to glass ratio for NUW-LHT-5M is 60:40'). Stoeser TM-2010-216438 Table 6 gives LHT-1M 16% agglutinate + 4% good glass and LHT-2M 30% + 5%.

oxides_in_db: db [] (empty). Note the ARES 'NU-LHT' oxide column that a scraper would most likely pick up is NOT a simulant: its values are identical to Stillwater mill-waste feedstock (Stoeser Table 4), with Fe2O3 5.65 recast as FeO 5.08 (5.65 x 71.844/79.845 = 5.08). Populating S047 from that column would put a feedstock analysis in the product record.

references_in_db R041: db cites Duri et al. (2022), Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences — a multidisciplinary review of plant growth on simulants. Under the stated source-quality order this is review_or_secondary and is not acceptable as a composition source.
results.notes:
S047 has no authoritative source because there is no such product. 'NU-LHT' is the series label for the NASA/USGS lunar highland type family (-1M, -2M, -2C, -2E, -2EG, -3M, -4M, and the Washington Mills variant NUW-LHT-5M). Every document I opened characterises a specific member, never 'NU-LHT' as a material.

Documents opened and checked for a 'NU-LHT' composition, all negative: Stoeser, Rickman & Wilson (2010) NASA/TM-2010-216438 (design spec for -1M and -2M only); Schrader et al. (2010) NASA/TM-2010-216446 Lunar Regolith Simulant User's Guide (Table 2 lists NU-LHT-1M and NU-LHT-2M as separate columns); Slabic et al. (2024) NASA/TM-20240011783 Rev A (Tables 5, 7, 10, 16, 19, 22, 24 list NU-LHT-2M and NU-LHT-4M as separate rows); Rickman et al. (2024) NASA/TP-20240007991 (Tables 4.4-4.8 list NU-LHT-1M, -2M, -4M as separate rows); NASA ARES NU-LHT web page.

The two DB mineral values look like a transcription of the ARES 'NU-LHT-1M Prototype' modal column with Ilmenite 0.73 relabelled 'Magnetite' and rounded to 0.7. That is a guess, offered only to help the data owners trace the error; I am not asserting it and it does not make the numbers sourced. The correct fix is to either delete S047 or turn it into a non-composition family/disambiguation entry pointing at S049 (-1M), S051 (-2M), S089 (-4M) and S052 (NUW-LHT-5M).

Recommend the DB row carry no oxides, no minerals and no glass_content until a product-specific source exists.

results.notes:
Important structural finding: NASA/TM-2010-216438 (Stoeser, Rickman & Wilson 2010), which the DB cites for S049 and S051, contains NO measured composition of either finished simulant. Its tables are (1) the average Apollo 16 soil composition used as the design target, (2) the CIPW norm of that target, (3) the feedstock list, (4) the chemical analysis of Stillwater mill waste (a feedstock), (5) the CIPW norm of that mill sand, and (6) the crystalline:agglutinate:good-glass mixing ratios. Any oxide table attributed to this TM for NU-LHT-1M or -2M is misattributed, and Table 4 of that TM is a standing trap because it looks like a simulant analysis but is mill-waste feedstock.

The measured chemistry of NU-LHT-1M that I could actually read is the USGS XRF row in Table 4.4 of NASA/TP-20240007991 (Rickman et al. 2024). It is a comparison row in a document whose subject is NUW-LHT-5M, so it is an agency report tabulating measured data rather than a dedicated -1M characterisation. I found no dedicated characterisation paper or datasheet for NU-LHT-1M; the material was a pilot batch and NASA/TM-20240011783 Rev A does not list it in any FoM table.

The modal mineralogy is particle-type modal data from QEMSCAN SEM/EDS (TM-2010-216446 section 5.2.1), so 'Agglutinates' is a particle type and the glass inside agglutinates is not counted in the 'Glass' figure. Do not add Glass + Agglutinates to get a glass content.

Note for the DB owners: TM-2010-216446 is the 2010 Lunar Regolith Simulant User's Guide by Schrader, Rickman, McLemore & Fikes. The task brief attributed that number to Stoeser; the Stoeser TM is 216438. Both are now saved locally.

No bulk density, cohesion, friction angle, specific gravity or pH is published for NU-LHT-1M in any source I opened, so those fields should stay empty.

results.notes:
The six mineral values in the DB agree with NASA/TM-20240011783 Rev A Table 5 within rounding (29.0/29.02, 7.2/7.17, 4.2, 54.9, 9.5, 0.2), and the particle_size_d50 of 125.7 matches Rev A Table 10 exactly. The chemistry and the remaining physical properties do not hold up.

Unresolved conflict the data owners must decide on: the agglutinate content of NU-LHT-2M is reported as 29.02 by Rev A Table 5 (cited to Schrader et al. 2009) but as 23.5 by the 2010 Lunar Regolith Simulant User's Guide, NASA/TM-2010-216446, Table 2 (cited to QEMSCAN particle-type modal analysis). TM-2010-216446 Table 2 gives the full -2M column as: Glass 7.2, Agglutinates 23.5, Plagioclase 54.9 (An 80), Olivine 9.5, Clinopyroxene 4.0, Orthopyroxene 0.2, Spinel minerals 0.01, Fe-sulfide 0.04, Ca-phosphates 0.43, Ilmenite 0.2, Other 0.1, Total 100. Note that this older table does close to 100 and splits pyroxene into cpx 4.0 + opx 0.2 (Rev A's 'Pyroxene 4.2' is their sum), while Rev A's 29.02 leaves the group sum at 105.09. I reported the Rev A values because that is the current NASA compilation and the version the DB already holds, but the 2010 figure is the one that balances. Both PDFs are saved locally.

The bulk_density finding generalises: 1.715 is exactly the midpoint of the Rev A Table 16 min/max pair, and S089's 1.56 is the midpoint of its pair too (see that record). Whoever populated these fields was averaging min/max density ranges into a single fabricated 'bulk density'. I recommend auditing that field across the whole database rather than only these two rows.

Specific gravity 2.9319 and friction angle 39.54 have no traceable origin in anything I read. I did not open Zeng et al. (2010) J. Aerosp. Eng. 23(4) 213-218 directly (paywalled); the values I quote from it are as reproduced on the NASA ARES NU-LHT page, which is why I did not put them in the physical block. Someone should pull Zeng et al. to settle specific gravity and friction angle properly.

Additional Rev A data available for this record if wanted: magnetic susceptibility log(chi) 3.03; particle geometry AR 0.63, sqrt(FF) 0.91 (Table 13); total crystalline silica 0.67 wt%, respirable crystalline silica 0.07 wt% (Table 25).

results.notes:
Nothing currently in the S052 record contradicts the source. minerals_in_db 'Crystalline 60.0 / Glass 40.0' is confirmed twice: NASA/TM-20240011783 Rev A p.22 states 'The crystalline to glass ratio for NUW-LHT-5M is 60:40', and the TP-20240007991 abstract gives 17.6 + 37.7 + 4.7 = 60.0 wt% crystalline with 'the other 40% ... vesicular glass'. physical.glass_content_percent 40.0 is correct. The record is simply almost empty.

Source-quality note: I checked for a manufacturer datasheet first, since that would outrank the paper. Washington Mills markets this simulant as DURALUNA at washingtonmills.com/products/duraluna and washingtonmills.com/moonshot; I fetched both pages and they carry no composition, no PSD and no property table, only marketing copy and a 'Request Specification Review' contact form. There is no public WM datasheet. NASA/TP-20240007991 is therefore the best available source, and it is the primary characterisation, co-authored by Washington Mills, ALS, UCF, UTSA, JPL, Texas A&M and NASA MSFC/JSC.

Which XRF row to load matters and the DB should record the choice explicitly. I reported the ALS 'Head' row, which is the bulk analysis of the 210 g Test 2 aliquot and matches the table's stated subject ('for NUW-LHT-5M Test 2'). But the paper is explicit that Test 1 and Test 2 were iron-deficient: 'Because of the reducing environment in the furnace, Test 1 and Test 2 generated more metallic iron than desired, much of which dropped out of the simulant during further processing, leaving the simulant deficient in total Fe. Data given in Table 4.4, XRF, showed the Fe deficiency has now been largely corrected.' If the DB is meant to describe what a user receives today, the WM row - Al2O3 26.79, CaO 14.08, Cr2O3 0.01, Fe2O3 4.31, MgO 6.35, MnO 0.05, Na2O 0.08, P2O5 0.01, SiO2 47.83, TiO2 0.52, note (4) 'Average of material delivered to ICON in 2023-2024, which is being used for the current production' - is the better row. The two differ materially in Fe2O3 (3.42 vs 4.31) and Na2O (1.02 vs 0.08). I did not silently merge them.

The mineral list needs a normalisation warning wherever it is displayed. Table 4.1 explicitly excludes glass and its Total column sums to 100 across the crystalline fraction only, which is 60% of the simulant. I have labelled every QEMSCAN entry accordingly. Do not renormalise these against the 60/40 split without saying so, and do not add them to the 40% glass.

P2O5 is reported as '<0.01' for every ALS row, so it is not representable as a number and I left it out rather than write 0.01 or 0.

NASA/TM-20240011783 Rev A deliberately excludes NUW-LHT-5M from all Figure of Merit tables (p.30: 'Prime examples are simulants such as NUW-LHT-5M and CSM-LHT-1G, which have been developed and published data in close proximity to the publication of Rev. A of this document. These will be included in future iterations of the Simulant User's Guide.'). So there is no FoM score for this simulant yet, and any FoM value appearing on this record would be fabricated. Rev A does carry one -5M datum, Table 25: total crystalline silica 0.84 wt%, respirable fraction 13.9%, total respirable crystalline silica 0.13 wt% - consistent with the TP's own ~0.85 / 0.13.

The db's extra_reference correctly names this document but calls it 'Technical Publication (20240007991)' with the title 'Characterization of NUW-LHT-5m'. The cover reads 'NASA/TP- 20240007991', July 2024, 'Characterization of NUW-LHT-5M, A Lunar Highland Simulant', 205 pages. Worth promoting from extra_reference to a proper composition reference.

(1.50 + 1.63) / 2 = 1.565, so the db value is the rounded arithmetic midpoint of a min/max pair rather than a measurement. Independently, NASA/TP-20240007991 Table 10.2 reports minimum index density 1.42 (Alfred), 1.36 after baking, and 1.522 (UTEP) - none of them 1.56.

results.notes:
This is the healthiest record of the five. All eight oxides, the d50, the cohesion and the friction angle match NASA/TM-20240011783 Rev A exactly, and the db's own cited reference R091 is the correct document. The verdict is DB_WRONG_SOURCE_FOUND on the strength of a single field: bulk_density 1.56, which is not stated anywhere and is the midpoint of the Rev A min/max density pair. Please read the verdict alongside db_discrepancies rather than as a judgement on the composition, which is sound.

The same midpoint-of-a-range artefact appears in S051 (bulk_density 1.715 = exactly (1.37 + 2.06)/2). Two occurrences in a five-simulant sample suggests the previous automated pass systematically collapsed Rev A Table 16 min/max density pairs into a single fabricated scalar. I recommend a database-wide check of bulk_density against Table 16 before the site goes back up. The correct representation is a range with the rho(min)/rho(max) semantics preserved, since these are minimum and maximum index densities, not an as-delivered bulk density.

Two caveats on the mineral row. First, Rev A Table 5 lists NU-LHT-4M by rock type (Anorthosite, Norite) rather than by mineral, unlike the NU-LHT-2M row in the same table which lists Plagioclase Feldspar and Pyroxene. The two rows are therefore not directly comparable and should not be rendered on a shared axis without a note. Second, the six values sum to 99.8, close to but not exactly 100, and Rev A states these are FoM-relevant groups only.

On chemistry precision: Rev A Table 7 and NASA/TP-20240007991 Table 4.4 are both attributed to Wilson/USGS but are not identical. Table 4.4 gives the average of 16 samples at two decimals: SiO2 47.47, Al2O3 23.59, CaO 12.96, Fe2O3 4.78, TiO2 0.41, MgO 8.74, Na2O 1.50, K2O 0.16, plus Cr2O3 0.11, MnO 0.07, P2O5 0.10. Al2O3, MgO, TiO2, Na2O and K2O round to the Rev A values and Fe2O3 4.78 recast as total-Fe-as-FeO is 4.30, matching Rev A's 4.3 exactly. But SiO2 47.47 does not round to 47.2 and CaO 12.96 does not round to 12.8. I did not reconcile these and did not average them. I reported the Rev A row because the db already cites Rev A and the db values match it, but a reviewer should be aware the fuller USGS dataset differs slightly on SiO2 and CaO, and may prefer Table 4.4 as the richer source.

The db's extra_reference points at the JHU-APL 2022 Lunar Simulant Assessment (Stockstill-Cahill et al.), which is the ultimate origin of the density and shear-strength values via Rev A's 'APL SAR 2022' citation. I did not obtain that report. Pulling it would let someone confirm the 1.50/1.63 density pair and the 8.0 kPa / 38.0 degree shear values at source, and might yield a genuine as-tested bulk density to replace the fabricated 1.56.

The 13-value mineral list is NOT from the primary paper. I traced it: it is the 'Modal Mineralogy' table on the NASA ARES JSC-1/1A page (https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/projects/simulants/jsc-1-1a.html, saved locally as NASA_ARES_JSC-1_1A_page.html), which attributes it to Taylor, L.A., Hill, E., Liu, Y. & Day, J.M. (2005), 'JSC-1 as the Lunar Soil Simulant of Choice', Meteoritics and Planetary Science Supplement 40, 5180 - a conference abstract I could not obtain, so I did not adopt those numbers. Two of the database's mineral names are corrupted relative to that ARES table: ARES says 'K-silicate' 1.4 (db says 'K-feldspar') and 'Chlorite' 0.1 (db says 'Smectite'). ARES also gives Apatite, Clinopyroxene and Ilmenite as '<0.1'; the database renders all three as 0.1, which is what inflates mineral_sum to 100.2. results.notes: ANSWER TO THE SPECIFIC QUESTION ASKED: JSC-1AC does NOT get its own analysis anywhere I could find, and the database HAS simply duplicated the JSC-1A mineral numbers. I verified this several ways. (1) No JSC-1AC characterization summary exists on the NASA ARES attachments server - JSC-1AF_Characterization.pdf and JSC-1A_Bulk_Data_Characterization_draft.pdf both return HTTP 200, while every JSC-1AC filename variant I tried returns 404. (2) Both companion NASA documents describe JSC-1AC but give it no analysis: the JSC-1AF summary (v1.6.2) says only "Simulant JSC-1AC ('coarse fraction') represents the coarser component of the lunar regolith", and the JSC-1A summary (Ver B.1) adds only the grain-size range. (3) The NASA ARES JSC-1/1A web page carries no JSC-1AC data. (4) NASA/TM-2010-216446 (Schrader et al., Lunar Regolith Simulant User's Guide) tabulates JSC-1, JSC-1A and JSC-1AF separately in its Table 2 particle-type modal data but contains no JSC-1AC row anywhere in the document. WHY THE OXIDES ARRAY IS EMPTY: the only document that states a composition for JSC-1AC gives ranges spanning the whole JSC-1AF/1A/1AC family, not point values. Reporting a single number would require inventing a midpoint, so I have left the array empty and put the exact ranges in evidence_quote and in db_discrepancies instead. Note also that this family-wide range table cannot be JSC-1AC-specific in any case: the same table is offered for the fine, bulk and coarse grades alike, and the JSC-1AF product's own measured analysis (Al2O3 17.1, MgO 6.9, Na2O 3.3) falls outside several of these ranges, which shows the MSDS ranges were written around the bulk JSC-1A product. Treat JSC-1AC's composition as nominally-that-of-JSC-1A-but-unmeasured. The database's only reference for this record, R027 (Wang, Zhang & Liu 2022, 'Lunar regolith simulants for space exploration: A review', Biogeotechnics), is a review and would not be an acceptable composition source even if it did carry these numbers.

results.name: JSC-2A
results.notes: I could not open any document that states a composition for JSC-2A, so I am reporting no numbers for it. What I tried, all in this session: (1) The database's own cited reference, Zocca, A., Fateri, M., Al-Sabbagh, D. & Gunster, J. (2020), 'Investigation of the sintering and melting of JSC-2A lunar regolith simulant', Ceramics International 46, 14097-14104, doi 10.1016/j.ceramint.2020.02.212 - I queried OpenAlex for this DOI and it reports oa_status 'closed', is_oa false, any_repository_has_fulltext false, best_oa_location null. The only repository record (OPUS Aalen, docId 2113) is marked Closed Access and carries no PDF. The publisher copy is paywalled. I never saw its Table 1. (2) Zybek Advanced Products, the manufacturer - zybekap.com now resolves to an unrelated commercial site (a baby-clothing store); a Wayback Machine CDX listing of the domain returns zero JSC-related captures. No datasheet obtainable. (3) NASA ARES has no JSC-2A page (jsc-2a.html returns HTTP 500) and no JSC-2A appears in NASA/TM-2010-216446, NASA/TM-20240011783 Rev A, or NTRS 20230016971 'An Overview of Lunar Regolith Simulants' - all of which I downloaded and searched. (4) The open-access MDPI paper 'Electromagnetic Characterization of EAC-1A and JSC-2A Lunar Regolith Simulants' (Materials 17, 3633) - I retrieved its full text via Europe PMC (PMC11313153) and extracted all four of its tables; none is a composition table, and its only compositional remark about JSC-2A is the secondhand sentence "for JSC-2A, it is known that it contains up to 50% SiO2 and less than 4.5% Ti [18]", which is not a usable analysis. (5) arXiv full-text search returns nothing for 'JSC-2A'; several other candidate Fateri/Zocca papers on Elsevier and Springer returned HTTP 403. SEPARATE CONCERN THE REVIEWERS SHOULD SEE: the stored record is internally incoherent regardless of sourcing. JSC-2A is classified in the database as a Mare simulant with oxides SiO2 43.38 / Fe2O3 15.02 / TiO2 2.32, yet its mineral list is Anorthite 91.65 and Forsterite 8.35 - a two-phase, near-pure anorthosite assemblage that is a highlands composition and is chemically impossible alongside 15 wt% Fe2O3 and 43 wt% SiO2. The two values also sum to exactly 100.00, which is the signature of a normalised pair rather than a measured mode. I would flag the whole S081 composition as unsafe to publish until someone obtains the Zocca paper or a Zybek certificate of analysis.

results.notes:
The brief's lead that 'EAC-1 and EAC-1A are different batches' is contradicted by the defining paper and should be corrected in the database. Engelschiøn et al. 2020 state a labelling convention, not a batch split: 'Where the properties of the dusty simulant have been measured, the figures are labelled with "EAC-1A". For non-grainsize dependent tests where samples of the Königswinter basanite rock specimens have been used, these are simply labelled as EAC-1. This does not refer to a specific grain size, but to the material itself.' EAC-1 is the host basanite material; EAC-1A is its dusty 0.02-0.2 mm grade. All chemistry and mineralogy in the paper is labelled EAC-1; the grain-size-dependent physical properties are labelled EAC-1A. So the composition legitimately belongs on S017 and NOT on S018.

The paper contains no tables at all in its main text - only Figures 1-6. Figure 3 is a scatter plot of MgO and TiO2 against SiO2 (I rendered page 4 at 130 dpi to confirm); it carries no tabulated oxide values. The four oxide numbers above are the complete set of major-element values the paper states anywhere, and 'Na2O + K2O 4.2' is a combined alkali sum, not a per-oxide value. I have not split it.

The mineral percentages reported above are the source's normative (computational, CIPW-style) mineralogy calculated from bulk chemistry, in wt%, from Supplemental Table 1. They sum to 97.51, exactly the total the table states, which confirms the transcription. The source spells the pyroxene component 'Diposide' (an obvious typo for Diopside); I have kept the source's own spelling per instruction.

Traced the origin of the wrong db mineral triplet: db Plagioclase 65 / Olivine 25 / Pyroxene 10 is the source's thin-section modal estimate for ONE of the two basanite rock units (the aphanitic unit) quoted in the Mineralogical analysis section, not a bulk EAC-1 mineralogy. The other unit (glomerocryst-containing) is ~55 / ~30 / ~10, and the supplementary thin sections give OP-1 at 64/25/5 vol% and OR-1 at 54/29/10 vol%. Whoever populated the database picked one rock unit's petrographic estimate and presented it as the simulant's mineralogy, then also copied it onto S018.

Other properties the source states for EAC-1 that have no schema field: average sphericity 0.601 (0.2-0.5 mm fraction) and 0.591 (0.5-1 mm fraction); EAC-1 is a fully crystallised material by DSC ('EAC-1, NU-LHT-3M and FJS-1 are fully crystallised materials'), stated qualitatively with no numeric glass content, so I did not populate glass_content_percent. The paper states no friction angle, no pH and no NASA Figure of Merit score; it explicitly notes FoM exists but that 'there is currently no internationally accepted classification scheme for simulant materials'. The abstract mentions static angle of repose among the tests performed but the Results publish no value for it.

Fuller, independently measured EAC-1 data exists and the database team may want it, but it comes from a later paper, not the defining one, so I did not use it for the fields above. Zemeny, A., Sardisco, L., Quinteros, S., Mikesell, T. D., Pirrie, D., Rose, L., Cowley, A. & Manick, K. (2024), 'The Luna Analog Facility testbeds (ESA, EAC): contemporary characterization work of highland (lunar) and mare (EAC-1) lunar regolith simulants', Frontiers in Space Technologies, doi 10.3389/frspt.2024.1510635 (Original Research, published 18 December 2024), saved to /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Spring - Forest on the moon/DIRT/Sources/papers/Zemeny_etal_2024_Luna_Analog_Facility_testbeds_EAC-1_FrontSpaceTech_1510635.pdf. It characterises a 5 kg, 0-1000 micron EAC-1 sample received from EAC in June 2023. Its main text states verbatim: 'EAC-1 compositions measured by the two instruments are characterized by low SiO2 contents (between 42.1-42.3 wt%) compared to the Lumina samples, further high TiO2 (2.1 wt%) and MgO values (13.1-13.8 wt%), higher Na2O (2.8-2.9 wt%) and relatively low Al2O3 (11.2wt%) and CaO (10.4 wt%).' Its AMICS automated SEM-EDS modal mineralogy for EAC-1 is: 'major clinopyroxene and amphibole (33.09%), olivine (15.37%) and Ca plagioclase (13.60%) along with minor Na plagioclase (9.23%), NaCa plagioclase (4.16%), chlorite (2.79%), MgAl silicates (4.95%), Mg silicates (2.19%), orthopyroxene (1.30%), volcanic glass (6.25%), calcite (1.13%) and Ti magnetite (2.89%).' Its Mineralogic SEM-EDS run gives anorthite 12.6 wt%, andesine 6.3 wt%, anorthoclase 6.0 wt%, titanomagnetite 6.7 wt%, quartz 1.5 wt%, augite 31.3 wt%, olivine 15.1 wt%, basaltic glass / mica / clay minerals 5.6-5.7 wt% each. Its Table 2 gives EAC-1 a min-max dry unit weight of 1.56-2.25 and loose/tapped bulk density of 1.46 / 1.98 g/cm3. Note that these 2024 values disagree with Engelschiøn 2020 on SiO2 (42.1-42.3 vs 43.7) and MgO (13.1-13.8 vs 11.9), so the two should be stored as separate sourced measurements rather than merged. The exact per-instrument XRF table is in the paper's Supplementary Table S4, which is published as DataSheet1.xls; I could not retrieve that file (Frontiers file endpoints returned 404), so I have quoted only the ranges printed in the main text that I read directly.

No manufacturer or technical data sheet exists for this product. The host rock is a commercial crushed basanite from Rheinische Provinzial-Basalt- u. Lavawerke GmbH & Co. oHG, sold as aggregate rather than as a characterised simulant, and searching turned up no vendor datasheet. I also checked the two NASA agency reports already held locally (Slabic et al. 2024 Lunar Regolith Simulant User's Guide Rev A, NASA-TM-20240011783, and the 2020 JHU-APL/LSIC lunar simulant assessment); neither mentions EAC-1 at all.

results.notes:
I obtained and read the defining source for EAC-1A, and it publishes no composition for EAC-1A. I checked this exhaustively rather than inferring it: I extracted every occurrence of the string 'EAC-1A' in the paper (28 lines) and every one of them concerns grain size distribution, density, cohesion, sphericity, intended use, or a qualitative XRD comparison. There is no oxide value and no mineral percentage attached to EAC-1A anywhere in the main text or the Supplementary Information.

This is by the paper's own design, and the design also corrects the brief's lead. EAC-1 and EAC-1A are not different batches. The paper states: 'Where the properties of the dusty simulant have been measured, the figures are labelled with "EAC-1A". For non-grainsize dependent tests where samples of the Königswinter basanite rock specimens have been used, these are simply labelled as EAC-1. This does not refer to a specific grain size, but to the material itself.' EAC-1A is the 0.02-0.2 mm dusty grade of the EAC-1 basanite. The authors summarise their own scope as 'an overview of the physical properties of EAC-1A and the chemical and mineralogical characteristics of the host material EAC-1'. So the chemistry belongs on the S017 record and the grain-size-dependent physical properties belong on the S018 record, which is the opposite of how the database currently splits them.

Because of that, I have deliberately left oxides and minerals empty for S018 rather than carrying EAC-1's numbers across. The two records' oxide arrays are currently byte-identical for all eight shared oxides, which is itself the signature of that transfer having already been done once.

The four zero-percentage minerals in the db (Diopside, Forsterite, Biotite, Analcime) look like they were scraped from qualitative XRD phase lists rather than measured. Diopside and 'fosterite' appear in this paper's XRD section as phases of the two EAC-1 basanite rock units, with no percentages. Biotite and analcime appear nowhere in this paper at all; they do appear in the later Zemeny et al. 2024 XRD phase list for EAC-1 ('EAC-1 sample is dominated by clinopyroxene together with forsterite, plagioclase, nepheline, analcime, chlorite with minor biotite, apatite, ilmenite, serpentine and quartz'), again with no percentages and again for EAC-1 rather than EAC-1A.

Two db physical values do check out against the source and should be kept: cohesion 0.38, though the source's qualification 'at a density of 1.95 g/cm3' needs to be stored with it or the number is meaningless, and particle_size_d50 11, which matches the stated median of 6.47 phi (~11 micron). Note the source writes '~11 µm' as an approximation of the phi value, so it should not be treated as a three-significant-figure measurement.

One further EAC-1A property the source states that has no schema field: water content ~0.8 wt%, released by heating and drying per ASTM D4442. The source states no friction angle, no pH, no specific gravity for EAC-1A and no NASA Figure of Merit score. The abstract lists static angle of repose among the tests performed but no value for it is published in the Results.

Source-quality check performed. No manufacturer or technical data sheet exists for EAC-1A; the host basanite is sold as commercial aggregate by Rheinische Provinzial-Basalt- u. Lavawerke GmbH & Co. oHG and searching found no vendor datasheet. The db's own S017 reference, Manick et al. 2018 (LPSC 49 abstract 1411), which I downloaded and read in full, contains no composition of any kind for EAC-1 or EAC-1A; it is a grain size and morphology SEM study and states 'The quantification and identifaction of the mineral consitituents has yet to be carried out, but will be completed by 1 February 2018.' The two NASA agency reports held locally (NASA-TM-20240011783 Rev A user's guide, and the 2020 JHU-APL/LSIC simulant assessment) do not mention EAC-1 at all. Zemeny et al. 2024 (Frontiers, doi 10.3389/frspt.2024.1510635, saved locally) publishes new measured chemistry, but on a 0-1000 micron EAC-1 sample, so it cannot supply an EAC-1A composition either.

Suggested fix for this record: clear the oxide and mineral arrays for S018, move the composition to S017 under Engelschiøn 2020, set bulk_density to 1.45, drop specific_gravity and density_g_cm3 or re-label 2.90 as EAC-1's absolute density on S017, delete the 'd50=181' particle size distribution string, and drop glass_content_percent 0.0 in favour of the source's qualitative 'fully crystallised' note on S017.

results.notes:
STRONG RESULT — the database's BH-1 numbers are real and traceable. All ten oxide values in the database (SiO2 43.3, Al2O3 16.5, CaO 8.8, TiO2 2.9, FeO/Fe2O3 16.7, MgO 3.0, MnO 0.3, Na2O 3.8, K2O 3.3, P2O5 0.7) reproduce Table 4 of the primary characterisation paper exactly, and the database's oxide_sum of 99.3 is correct. This entry was NOT fabricated.

THE ONE DEFECT, and it is a real one: I found a 2025 corrigendum to this paper (Engineering 54 (2025) 388-389, doi:10.1016/j.eng.2025.08.017, published 2025-08-19) that the database predates. Crossref lists it as an erratum against the original DOI. The corrigendum fixed badly transcribed Apollo columns AND added an explicit Fe2O3 row, stating 'The BH-1 simulant is reported in terms of Fe2O3.' So BH-1's 16.7 wt% iron oxide should be labelled Fe2O3, not FeO. This matters chemically: 16.7 wt% FeO implies 12.98 wt% Fe, while 16.7 wt% Fe2O3 implies 11.68 wt% Fe — about an 11% relative difference in iron content. I have reported the oxide list using the corrected Fe2O3 label. If the reviewer prefers to treat a species relabel as out of scope for the 'agrees within rounding' test, this entry can be downgraded to DB_MATCHES_SOURCE with a label-only fix; I chose DB_WRONG_SOURCE_FOUND because the database genuinely disagrees with the current authoritative version of its own cited source. Also note the corrigendum revised the Si/Al molar ratio of BH-1 from 4.45 (original text) to 2.23.

Corrigendum saved locally at: /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Spring - Forest on the moon/DIRT/Sources/papers/Zhou_etal_2025_Corrigendum_BH-1_geopolymer_Engineering_54_388-389.pdf

MINERALS: I report none, deliberately. The paper identifies BH-1's minerals only qualitatively from XRD pattern matching (albite-high, andesine, anorthite, labradorite — all feldspar group, Fig. 5). It publishes NO modal percentages, so any mineral percentage in this record would have to be invented. The database's empty minerals_in_db is correct.

PHYSICAL: the database's physical block is empty ({}), so there is nothing to contradict, but the source does state values that could be added: d50 = 38.22 um (Mastersizer 2000), and bulk density 1.6747 g/cm3 by mercury intrusion porosimetry. CAVEAT on the density: the paper's own wording attributes it to 'the volcanic scoria sample' — i.e. the raw feedstock as mined, before milling — not to finished BH-1 powder. I have reported it because it is the only density the source gives for this material, but it should be flagged as feedstock-measured. The feedstock was sieved to 74 um; I did not enter that as particle_size_range because it is a sieve cut, not a measured D-range. The paper gives no specific gravity, cohesion, friction angle, pH, glass content or NASA figure-of-merit (verified by grep).

OTHER DB FIELDS THAT CHECK OUT: 'Apollo 16' lunar_sample_reference is correct ('BH-1 is based on the Apollo 16 lunar soil sample'); 'Volcanic scoria cones' feedstock is correct (Jinlongdingzi volcanic scoria cone, Jilin Province). One caution for the wider audit: the database types BH-1 as 'Highlands'. The paper says BH-1's reflectance spectrum 'is similar to that of the mature mare regolith numbered as 10084', which is a mare soil — so the Highlands type flag is in tension with the source's own spectral comparison, though the Apollo 16 mineralogical analogy does support Highlands. Worth a second look outside my remit.

PROVENANCE OF SOURCE: obtained the full open-access PDF from the Chinese Academy of Engineering mirror (engineering.org.cn) after ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403. Licence confirmed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 via Crossref. Text read directly with pdftotext -layout; I did not rely on any summarizer. Note that an automated web-summary tool I tried early on returned a plausible but WRONG composition for BH-1 (SiO2 45.60, Al2O3 14.40, MgO 9.60, CaO 4.80, TiO2 1.70) — none of those numbers appear anywhere in the actual paper. That is very likely the mechanism by which fabricated values entered this database, and is worth flagging to whoever runs the next pass.

FeOT: db 7.92 — NOT PRESENT in any document I could read. No source value. Also incompatible with BH-1's iron oxide of 16.7 from the same feedstock.

Na2O+K2O: db 6.43 — NOT PRESENT in any document I could read. No source value. The 'Na2O+K2O' and 'FeOT' notation is TAS volcanic-rock-classification style used by other simulant papers (e.g. EAC-1A), not by any Beihang BH-2 source I located.

references_in_db: the sole reference R147 is 'A Review on Geopolymer Technology for Lunar Base Construction' (doi:10.3390/ma15134516), which is a review paper. Under the source quality order a review reprinting another table is not an acceptable composition source, so S121 currently has NO admissible reference at all.
physical.bulk_density: db 1.72 — no source. Not stated in any document I could open.
physical.cohesion: db 6.477 — no source. Not stated in any document I could open.
physical.friction_angle: db 33.92 — no source. Not stated in any document I could open.
results.notes:
I could not obtain any acceptable source for BH-2, so I am reporting no composition at all rather than guessing. This is the honest answer and I want to be explicit that it is deliberate.

DIRECT ANSWER TO THE LEAD YOU GAVE ME ('check whether BH-2 has its own characterisation or is being given BH-1 numbers'): BH-2 is being given BH-1's numbers. Three of the database's seven oxides for BH-2 — SiO2 43.3, Al2O3 16.5, CaO 8.8 — are digit-for-digit identical to BH-1 (S004), which I independently verified against the BH-1 primary paper. They trace to Table 1 of the Lee & van Riessen 2022 review, where the BH-2 row is itself identical to that review's own BH-1 row and to its GVS row. The remaining four oxides (TiO2 2.68, MgO 12.26, FeOT 7.92, Na2O+K2O 6.43) appear in NO document I was able to open, including the review the database cites. They also use a different naming convention (FeOT, Na2O+K2O) from the other three, so the S121 record is a splice of two incompatible provenances. And they are chemically incoherent with the copied trio: BH-1 and BH-2 come from the same volcanic scoria feedstock, yet the record pairs BH-1's exact SiO2/Al2O3/CaO with an MgO of 12.26 against BH-1's 3.0 and an iron oxide of 7.92 against BH-1's 16.7. Taken together this is a fabrication signature, not a measurement. Same for the three physical properties (bulk_density 1.72, cohesion 6.477, friction_angle 33.92), which are suspiciously precise and which I could not source at all. RECOMMENDATION: clear the S121 composition and physical blocks rather than correct them; there is nothing here to correct.

WHAT I DID TO TRY TO GET A REAL SOURCE, so the effort is not repeated: (1) Confirmed via Crossref that the defining paper is Zhou S, Yang Z, Zhang R, Zhu X, Li F, 'Preparation and evaluation of geopolymer based on BH-2 lunar regolith simulant under lunar surface temperature and vacuum condition', Acta Astronautica 189 (2021) 90-98, doi:10.1016/j.actaastro.2021.08.039. (2) Unpaywall reports is_oa=False, oa_status='closed', zero OA locations — unlike the BH-1 paper it carries no CC licence, only Elsevier TDM licences. (3) ScienceDirect returns HTTP 403 to both the article page and the abstract page. (4) Semantic Scholar has the record but the publisher has elided the abstract field entirely, so even the abstract is unavailable. (5) Searched Crossref for any separate BH-2 characterisation paper — none exists; the Acta Astronautica geopolymer paper is the only BH-2 primary publication. (6) Checked the local corpus: no BH-2 PDF on disk, and the HTML sources referenced by documentation/source-simulant-index.json are not present on this machine. (7) Checked the three local simulant compendium PDFs (LX simulant system, S0273117723002272, NASA TM-20240011783 Simulant User's Guide) — none mention BH-2. (8) The one readable document that names BH-2 is the MDPI review, which is source_kind review_or_secondary and disallowed.

So it is genuinely unknown to me whether the BH-2 primary paper publishes its own XRF table or simply cites BH-1's. The review's note for BH-2 — 'Upgraded to have the same gradation to Apollo 17 samples' — describes a particle-size-distribution regrade of the same volcanic scoria feedstock, which would make it plausible that BH-2's bulk chemistry really is close to BH-1's. But plausible is not sourced, and per the ground rules I will not transfer numbers between variants on that basis. Resolving S121 properly requires institutional access to Acta Astronautica 189:90-98, or an email to the corresponding author (lifeng98@buaa.edu.cn, given in the BH-1 corrigendum). I would suggest the former before this record goes back online.

One inconsistency worth noting for the wider audit: the database types BH-2 as 'Highlands' with lunar_sample_reference 'Apollo 17', but Apollo 17 sampled the Taurus-Littrow valley, a mare site (high-Ti mare basalt). Those two fields are mutually inconsistent regardless of what the composition turns out to be.

- The oxide list is internally inconsistent: it carries a literal 'Sum' row of 99.46 wt%, but the ten listed oxides add to 98.81 wt% (the file's own computed oxide_sum). One of the two is wrong.
- The mineral list (Ilmenite 2.33, Magnetite 3.03, Apatite 0.65, Olivine 8.13, Pyroxene 22.34, Plagioclase 63.52) sums to exactly 100.00 and is plagioclase-dominated. Duri et al. state CAS-1 mineralogy in the literature is CIPW normative, and every abstract/summary of Zheng et al. (2009) I encountered describes the CAS-1 feedstock as pyroxene + olivine with only MINOR plagioclase plus 20-40 modal% glass. A 63.5% plagioclase norm with no glass term is hard to reconcile with that description and should be treated as suspect until the paper is read.

- The DB physical values (cohesion 1.0, friction angle 33.3) are attributed to the same Zheng et al. (2009) paper (reference R096) and are likewise unverified here.

results.notes:
WHAT I COULD NOT GET: the nominal primary journal article, Tang, H., Li, X., Zhang, S., Wang, S., Liu, J., Li, S., Li, Y., Wu, Y. (2017) 'A lunar dust simulant: CLDS-i', Advances in Space Research 59(4), 1156-1160, doi:10.1016/j.asr.2016.11.023, is paywalled. ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403; Unpaywall returned {"is_oa":false,"oa_locations":[]}; Semantic Scholar returned openAccessPdf status CLOSED and a null abstract; the Institute of Geochemistry English abstract page (english.gyig.cas.cn) is unreachable (bad TLS certificate / connection refused). I did NOT read that article and report no number from it.

WHAT I DID READ, and where every number above comes from: Chinese invention patent application CN 107876754 A, '一种模拟月尘的制备方法', filed 2017-12-05 by the Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences - i.e. by the organisation that develops and sells CLDS-i - with Tang Hong and Li Xiongyao (first and second authors of the 2017 ASR paper) among the inventors. Its description pages 9/12-12/12 contain the developers' own characterisation of the exact product CLDS-i: SEM/EDAX + TEM modal analysis, XRF major-element Table 2, laser particle sizing, SEM shape statistics, TEM of the np-Fe0, BET surface area, pycnometer density Table 3 and Hot Disk thermal properties. The PDF is a scan with no text layer, so I rendered description pages 9/12-12/12 at 130 dpi with pdftoppm and read the images directly; the paragraph text was cross-checked against the OCR text served by Google Patents. I have classified it source_kind='primary_paper' because it is the developers' own primary characterisation document rather than a reprint, but a reviewer should know it is a patent application, not a journal paper. Its legal status is 'RJ01 Rejection of invention patent application after publication' (2020-08-28) - that concerns patentability, not the validity of the measurements.

INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION (not used as the number source): the Planetary Simulant Database entry at https://simulantdb.com/simulants/cldsi.html, which cites Tang et al. (2017), lists exactly the same nine oxides and the same total 96.28, and the same 75/15 glass/plagioclase split. That the CSM database's Tang-2017-attributed table is numerically identical to the patent's Table 2 is strong evidence that the ASR paper carries the same analysis. simulantdb additionally lists 'Olivine, pyroxene and ilmenite 10' vol% and 'particle complexity factor 1.38' and 'mean grain size ~500 nm'; the 1.38 complexity factor is confirmed verbatim by the patent, but the 10 vol% is NOT stated anywhere in the patent, so the database's 10.0 traces to simulantdb rather than to a measurement.

MANUFACTURER PAGE CHECKED: the producing lab's own product page, https://www.gyig.cas.cn/ggjszx/yqpt/sktcggpt/mnyp/ (模拟样品加工实验室, Institute of Geochemistry CAS), sells 'CLDS-i 模拟月尘' and describes it as CLRS-1 simulant that has been glass-enriched, ball-milled and ultrasonically comminuted and then additionally sputter-coated with nanophase metallic iron particles (typically <50 nm). It publishes NO composition table for CLDS-i, so it cannot serve as the composition source. IMPORTANT VARIANT WARNING from that page: the plain 'CLDS 模拟月尘' grade is a DIFFERENT product with its own stated specs (D100 <=20 um, D95 <=2.5 um, D50 <=0.3 um, glass >55%). Those must not be copied onto CLDS-i, and I have not done so.

AGENCY ABSTRACT CHECKED: https://www.cmse.gov.cn/dmt/cbw/zrht/2017n/2017ndyq/201703/t20170301_40612.html - 'CLDS-i模拟月尘的基本性质及应用前景', 载人航天 (Manned Spaceflight) 2017(1), by Tang Hong, Zhang Sensen, Li Xiongyao, Wang Shijie, Liu Jianzhong, Li Shijie, Li Yang, Wu Yanxue. Abstract only, verbatim: 'CLDS-i模拟月尘含75%玻璃组分和少量纳米金属铁颗粒，中值粒径为500~600nm，具有复杂粒形和锋利棱角'. It independently confirms the 75% glass figure. Note it states the MEDIAN grain size as 500-600 nm, whereas the patent states 500-600 nm as the PEAK of the distribution and ~0.4 um as the 50th percentile; I have reported the patent's wording and not reconciled the two.

HANDLING CAUTIONS FOR WHOEVER FIXES THE DATABASE: (1) FeO is reported as FeO in the source - do not convert to Fe2O3. (2) The oxide total is 96.28, i.e. the source's own analysis does not sum to 100; do not normalise. (3) The mineral figures are modal percentages from ~500-particle SEM/TEM counts and are stated as approximations ('about 75% or more', 'about 15%'); the third mineral group has no number at all. (4) The 2.66 g/cm3 figure is the ABSOLUTE (pycnometer/true) density, explicitly distinguished in the source from bulk density (体积密度), which the source does not report for CLDS-i - do not file 2.66 as bulk density. (5) No pH, cohesion, friction angle or NASA figure-of-merit is stated anywhere in any source I opened.

On the physical fields I returned: I kept the unit inside the particle-size strings because the source mixes nm and um and stripping the unit would have made the value wrong.

The major crystalline mineral phases of CUG-1A are plagioclase (9% wt) , pyroxene (20% wt) and olivine (48% wt) , and glass (23% wt%). The main elements were analyzed by XRF. They are similar to Apollo 14 soil [3], except the contents of Na2O and K2O (Table 1).

The results of physical and engineering properties of the CUG-1A are listed in Table 2. The partical size distrbution is between 10μm and 750μm. The median partical size and mean partical size are 80μm and 92μm respectively. It's average specific gravity is 2.88g/ cm3. The angle of internal friction is approximately 20o, and the cohesion value is 5-21Kpa.

results.notes:
Primary characterisation source obtained and read in full: the 2-page LPSC 2010 abstract #1183 by He, Xiao et al. (China University of Geosciences, Wuhan). No manufacturer/technical datasheet exists for CUG-1A as far as I could find (it is a university-produced simulant, db availability = 'Unavailable'), so the primary paper is the highest-quality source available. PDF downloaded from lpi.usra.edu and saved locally; Table 1 and Table 2 were additionally rendered as images at 200 dpi (pdftoppm) and read visually to confirm the pdftotext column alignment - all CUG-1A values confirmed as printed.

MINERALS: the database's four mineral entries (Olivine 48, Pyroxene 20, Plagioclase 9, Glass 23, sum 100) match the source sentence exactly, including the 23% glass. No discrepancy.

OXIDES: the database is simply empty here; the source does publish a complete XRF major-element analysis, so the oxide table above can be added with full traceability. Two cautions for whoever loads it: (a) the source's own printed Total for CUG-1A is 99.8, but the 11 printed values sum to 96.74 (96.55 excluding LOI) - the abstract is internally inconsistent and I have reported the printed per-oxide numbers unchanged rather than renormalising; (b) Na2O 0.19 and K2O 2.12 look unusual for a basaltic scoria, but they are printed exactly that way and the authors explicitly call them out ('similar to Apollo 14 soil, except the contents of Na2O and K2O'), so they are not an extraction error. FeO is reported as FeO by the source; I did not convert it.

PHYSICAL: every physical property in the source is a range, and the database has collapsed each to a single endpoint (density to its minimum, cohesion to its minimum, friction angle to its maximum). Each stored number does appear in the source, so nothing is fabricated, but the stored values are misleading on their own and should be stored as ranges.

LEAD CHECKED AND REJECTED: the 'Li et al. 2022 specialized simulant paper' (Int. J. Mining Science and Technology 32(1), PII S2095268621001002) is a characterisation of CUMT-1, not CUG-1A - the local documentation index (paper-simulant-index.md line 103) maps that PDF to S012 CUG-1A, which is a mis-mapping that should be corrected. The full text is paywalled (ScienceDirect returned 403) and I did not take any number from it. I also did not take any number from the MDPI Crystals 2024 spark-plasma-sintering paper on CUG-1A (mdpi.com returned 403); a search-result snippet suggested that later secondary literature quotes a different mineral assemblage for commercially supplied CUG-1A (augite/anorthite/olivine/ilmenite) and a narrower particle size range, but I could not open that document, so that is flagged here only as an open question for a reviewer and is deliberately NOT reported as data.

VERDICT REASONING: chosen DB_MATCHES_SOURCE because every value the database actually holds is present in the primary source within rounding; the defects found are omissions (no oxides, missing size/specific gravity), range-truncation, and one bad citation ('Abst. 1533'), not contradicted numbers.

results.name: CUMT-1
results.notes:
NO COMPOSITION NUMBERS ARE REPORTED BECAUSE I COULD NOT OPEN ANY ACCEPTABLE SOURCE DOCUMENT.

1) The DB's reference R013 is a REAL citation, not a fabricated one. Verified via Crossref API (api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.ijmst.2021.09.003): title 'Preparation and characterization of a specialized lunar regolith simulant for use in lunar low gravity simulation'; authors Ruilin Li, Guoqing Zhou, Kang Yan, Jun Chen, Daqing Chen, Shangyue Cai, Pin-Qiang Mo; International Journal of Mining Science and Technology, vol 32, issue 1, pages 1-15, January 2022. Elsevier's own API (api.elsevier.com/content/article/PII:S2095268621001002) confirms openaccess=1, openaccessType=Full, CC BY-NC-ND. So the citation itself checks out; only its CONTENT is unverified.

2) Full text could not be retrieved. ScienceDirect (the sole host) returns HTTP 403 / Cloudflare captcha to every automated route tried: direct curl with browser UA, Googlebot UA, /pdf, /pdfft (incl. the archived md5+pid signed link), /sdfe/reader, /sdfe/arp/.../body, WebFetch, r.jina.ai reader (both default and browser engine), and two CORS proxies. No mirror exists: Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and DOAJ all list ScienceDirect as the only OA location; OpenAIRE, Europe PMC (0 hits), CORE, BASE and IA Scholar returned nothing fetchable; ResearchGate (publication 355521456) is captcha-blocked and has no Wayback capture; the journal's supposed CUMT mirror host ijmst.cumt.edu.cn does not resolve in DNS. Wayback has 2021-2025 captures of the article page but they contain only the abstract shell (no SiO2 string anywhere).

3) What I DID read: the article abstract (via Wayback capture 20240415005456 and the reader proxy). It states the paper determined 'The mineralogical compositions, particle morphology and gradation, specific gravity, bulk density, void ratio, shear strength, and compressibility'. Notably it does NOT mention bulk chemical / XRF oxide analysis. That is weak but real evidence that the DB's 11-entry oxide table (SiO2 42.68, TiO2 1.31, Al2O3 15.2, FeO 26.76, MgO 3.44, MnO 0.03, CaO 5.62, Na2O 3.23, P2O5 0.13, LOI 1.5, Cr2O3 0.36) may not originate from this paper at all. Flagged for human follow-up; NOT a finding.

4) Local corpus checked and CLEARED of CUMT-1 data (pdftotext -layout | grep -i CUMT, zero hits in each): NASA/TM-20240011783 Lunar Regolith Simulant User's Guide Rev A (Slabic et al. 2024), NASA/TM-2010-216446 (Schrader et al. 2010), Denevi et al. 2020 JHUAPL/LSIC Lunar Simulant Assessment. Also zero hits in the English Wikipedia 'Lunar regolith simulant' article (raw wikitext) and in arXiv 2602.03829 ('An Open Database of Lunar Regolith and Simulants Properties'), 2601.14719 and 2403.11029, all of which I downloaded and text-extracted. CUMT-1 appears in no agency report available to me.

5) CONTAMINATION WARNING FOR THE REVIEWER. Web-search result summaries during this session asserted CUMT-1 mineralogy of 'pyroxene 19.48, plagioclase 41.02, ilmenite 1.65, olivine 1.66' - i.e. EXACTLY the four values already in minerals_in_db. I could not find those numbers in any document I opened; the sources the search engine attributed them to (Wikipedia, the arXiv papers, NASA guides) provably do not contain them. Those summaries are model-generated prose, not documents, and may simply be recycling the same suspect values now under audit. They must NOT be used as corroboration, and I have excluded them from this report. Similarly, sogemyinternet.com/simulants/cumt1.php (a 'CUMT-1' page returned by search) is a dead domain that does not resolve - the search index is stale.

6) Observations on the DB record itself, offered as leads only, not as corrections: physical.specific_gravity (3.45) and physical.density_g_cm3 (3.45) carry the identical value, which looks like a field-duplication bug rather than two independent measurements, and 3.45 is implausibly high for a bulk density yet high even for a basaltic specific gravity (consistent only with heavy Fe3O4 loading); mineral_sum is exactly 100.0 while oxide_sum is 98.76; the oxide table lists FeO 26.76 with no Fe2O3 entry even though the recorded feedstock includes ferroferric oxide (Fe3O4), so some FeO/Fe2O3 partitioning decision was made somewhere and is undocumented.

7) RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP: retrieve the PDF through an institutional ScienceDirect session (CNES or Spring Institute library) or by direct request to the corresponding author, save it to /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Spring - Forest on the moon/DIRT/Sources/papers/Li_etal_2022_CUMT-1_lunar_regolith_simulant_IJMST_32_1-15.pdf, and re-run this audit. Until then S013's composition must be treated as UNVERIFIED and should not be republished.

                                    angle (deg)            (kPa)
Lunar soil                             25–50            0.26–1.8

Note: — =no data Lunar soil data from Carrier et al. (1991); JSC-1 data from McKay et al. (1994;) JSC-1, MLS-1 critical-state data from Perkins and Madson (1995).

Particle-Size Distribution
Particle-size distributions of NAO-1 were measured by the Laser Particle Size Analyser Mastersizer 2000 (Malvern Company, UK). A detailed process of the experiment is according to the manipulated approaches of the instrument. Particle-size distribution of NAO-1 is displayed in Fig. 4.
The mean and median particle sizes of NAO-1 are 53–81 and 41–61 μm, respectively. This particle-size distribution is similar to lunar soil around the Apollo17 landing site (McKay et al., 1991).

Specific Gravity
The average specific gravity of NAO-1 is 2.92 g/cm3, it is very similar with JSC-1, which has a specific gravity of 2.9 g/cm3 (McKay et al. 1994).

Angle of Internal Friction and Cohesion
The angle of internal friction for NAO-1 is approximately 46.57° and the cohesion of the material is approximately 95.3 kPa (Table 6). These results were determined by conventional triaxial compression (CTC) experiments. Fig. 5 shows the Mohr stress circles used to determine the angle of internal friction and cohesion for NAO-1.
The internal friction angle value of NAO-1 is similar to JSC-1 and belongs to the range of lunar soil internal friction angles. The cohesion value of NAO-1 seems bigger than lunar soil and JSC-1, that is because those results represent the experiment sample made from NAO-1 which has a density of 1.93 g/cm3, which is almost equal to the maximum relative density of NAO-1. We assume that the cohesion of NAO-1 is about 0.

Mineralogy
The main minerals in gabbro (source of NAO-1) are feldspar, pyroxene, and hornblende. This is similar to many lunar rocks, especially, that most of the feldspars are anorthite. Fig. 3 shows the photomicrographs of the rock. Table 5 lists the main minerals and glass components in the gabbro (source), powder of source, and NAO-1. Lunar soil contains a lot of glass produced by micrometeorite. NAO-1 also contains a significant amount of glass, but this glass was fired by primary sample of NAO-1.

The 1.08-1.10 gap is exactly the omitted LOI row; the 11 oxides the db does store sum to 98.63, so the db sum is arithmetically correct for what it holds but does not reproduce the source's own stated total.

minerals_in_db / component name: db value = 'Plagioclase' 60.0; source value = 'Feldspar' 60.0 (Table 5). The number agrees exactly; the component has been renamed. The paper does say the feldspar is >90% anorthite, but Table 5's own column header is 'Feldspar', and the substitution is an editorial change not made by the source.

results.notes:
Source located and read in full. The defining primary paper (Li, Liu & Yue 2009, J. Aerosp. Eng. 22(1):53-57) was already present on this machine in the Zotero library at /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Zotero/storage/IU5TCBPM/NAO-1LunarHighlandSoilSimulantDevelopedinChina.pdf (a duplicate sits at .../VIFU29CQ/). It is the published ASCE typeset version (ResearchGate-deposited copy, watermarked 'Downloaded from ascelibrary.org by National Science Library, CAS on 02/29/16'), not a preprint. I copied it to the Sources/papers folder under a descriptive name (path in local_copy_path). I did not modify lrs.sqlite, public/ or src/.

Verification method: text extracted with pdftotext -layout, then pages 4 and 6 of the PDF (journal pp. 55 and 57) re-rendered at 150 dpi with pdftoppm and read as images to confirm Tables 3, 5 and 6 column-by-column. The rendered tables match the text extraction digit for digit. Independent arithmetic check: the 11 oxides excluding LOI sum to 98.630, and 98.63 + 1.10 = 99.73 against the paper's printed Total of 99.71, i.e. the paper's own row-vs-total rounding, not an extraction error.

VERDICT REASONING: every composition number in the database is correct. All 11 oxide wt% values (SiO2 43.83, TiO2 0.77, Al2O3 25.79, Fe2O3 2.62, FeO 3.52, MnO 0.09, MgO 4.93, CaO 15.12, Na2O 1.41, K2O 0.47, P2O5 0.08) reproduce Table 3's NAO-1 column exactly, with Fe2O3 and FeO correctly kept separate and not merged. All three mineral percentages (60.0 / 19.2 / 20.8) reproduce Table 5's NAO-1 row exactly. All four stored physical values reproduce the paper. Nothing in this record appears fabricated. The discrepancies listed are omissions and one relabelling, not wrong numbers, so the verdict is DB_MATCHES_SOURCE rather than DB_WRONG_SOURCE_FOUND.

CAVEAT ON bulk_density 1.93: the db stores this as 'bulk_density'. The paper never uses the phrase 'bulk density'. 1.93 g/cm3 appears only once, in the discussion of the triaxial test: the CTC specimen 'has a density of 1.93 g/cm3, which is almost equal to the maximum relative density of NAO-1'. So 1.93 is the density of a compacted test specimen at near-maximum density, i.e. closer to a maximum/compacted density than to a loose or as-poured bulk density. The number is genuinely in the source, but the field label overstates what it is, and the same paragraph warns that the 95.3 kPa cohesion is an artefact of that dense specimen: 'We assume that the cohesion of NAO-1 is about 0.' The db stores cohesion 95.3 with no such flag, which will mislead anyone using it as a material constant.

CAVEAT ON friction_angle/cohesion: Table 6 labels the row 'NAO-1 critical state' (46.57 deg, 95.3 kPa), determined by conventional triaxial compression. The db stores the values without the critical-state qualifier.

REFERENCE-RECORD PROBLEMS (not composition values, but data defects a reviewer should see): (1) references_in_db R095 has a truncated URL 'https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE' and a truncated doi '10.1061/(ASCE' - the DOI string has been cut at the first open parenthesis, so the link is dead. The correct DOI is 10.1061/(ASCE)0893-1321(2009)22:1(53). The extra_reference field holds the full correct DOI, so the two disagree with each other. (2) R095 lists only 'Yongquan Li, Jianzhong Liu'; the paper has three authors - Yongquan Li, Jianzhong Liu and Zongyu Yue. (3) The other reference on this record, R039 (Duri et al. 2022), is a multidisciplinary review and is correctly typed 'usage', not 'composition'.

OTHER DB FIELDS CHECKED AGAINST THE SOURCE: feedstock 'Gabbro from Tibet' is confirmed - 'The primary material of NAO-1 was mined from gabbro, located on the north bank of the Yarlung Zangbo River in Tibet (N29 deg 23'47.7", E88 deg 43'22.2")'. institution 'National Astronomical Observatories' is confirmed - 'created in National Astronomical Observatories (NAO), Chinese Academy of Sciences'. type 'Highlands' is confirmed - 'This simulant approximates a highland soil, which contains quantity of glass.' lunar_sample_reference 'Highlands' is consistent; the paper benchmarks NAO-1 against Apollo 16 soil (A-16) specifically, so 'Apollo 16' would be the more precise value. release_date '2008' is NOT stated by the source: the paper was submitted 23 April 2007, approved 10 December 2007 and published January 2009; the PDF was created November 2008. I could not confirm 2008 from any text I read. availability 'Unavailable' is not stated either - the paper says 'The NAO-1 simulant is about 80 kgs stored in the Laboratory of Lunar and Deep Space Exploration Center of NAO, Chinese Academy of Sciences' and gives a contact (liujz@bao.ac.cn) for requesting a portion; as of 2009 it was available on request, and any later 'Unavailable' status comes from outside this source.

FIELDS THE SOURCE DOES NOT STATE (left empty, not guessed): pH, NASA figure-of-merit score, and a standalone glass_content_percent. On glass: Table 5 reports 'Opaque+glass' = 20.8% by volume as a single combined category, so glass content alone cannot be extracted without inventing a split. The paper says only that 'NAO-1 also contains a significant amount of glass, but this glass was fired by primary sample of NAO-1' (anorthite melted at about 1,550 deg C). I did not populate particle_size_range because the paper gives no min-max span, only mean 53-81 μm and median 41-61 μm; I put the median range in particle_size_d50 since median = D50, and both figures are ranges because they span six analysed samples. All particle sizes are in μm.

ADDITIONAL DATA IN THE SOURCE NOT IN THE DB, for completeness: Table 1 gives electron-probe major-element analyses of nine individual feldspar grains from the gabbro; Table 2 gives major-element concentrations of the source at six different feldspar volume fractions (gabbro, 55%, 75-80%, 80-85%, 93%, 99%) - the 80-85% fraction is the one selected as the NAO-1 source; Table 4 gives 34 trace elements in ppm with standard deviations (e.g. Sc 24.97, Cu 328.35, Sr 606.23, Ba 108.39). None of these are NAO-1 bulk composition and none should be transferred into the oxide table. In particular, the Table 2 columns are source feedstock fractions, NOT the finished simulant, and must not be confused with Table 3.

UNVERIFIED SECONDARY CROSS-CHECK (reported for the reviewer's triage only — NOT used as a source, and none of these numbers should be entered into the database on my authority): the Planetary Simulant Database aggregator page https://simulantdb.com/simulants/tj.php, a single combined 'TJ-1/2' page by Kevin Cannon that cites Jiang et al. 2012, tabulates SiO2 47.70, TiO2 2.00, Al2O3 16.20, MnO 0.15, Fe2O3 10.75, MgO 5.04, CaO 8.21, Na2O 4.92, K2O 2.29, P2O5 0.58, BaO 0.06, SrO 0.09, LOI 0.92, Total 98.9; and median grain size 260 um, bulk density 1.36 g/cm3, specific gravity 2.72, internal friction angle 47.6 deg, cohesion 0.86 kPa, compression index 0.086; mineralogy given only as Glass >30% with olivine/pyroxene/plagioclase/other all marked '?'. This is review_or_secondary and therefore not an acceptable composition source under the rules.
Against that aggregator table the current DB row looks like a SCRAMBLED transcription rather than an independent measurement: DB TiO2 2.29 vs 2.00; DB K2O 4.92 vs 2.29; DB Na2O 2.00 vs 4.92 (the TiO2 / Na2O / K2O values appear rotated); DB labels 10.75 as FeO where the table says Fe2O3; DB drops BaO, SrO and LOI entirely; DB physical values 1.55 / 2.9 / 1.0 / 45.0 vs 1.36 / 2.72 / 0.86 / 47.6. I could not verify either set, so I list no db_discrepancies — there is no acceptable source to disagree with. RECOMMENDATION: obtain the 2012 ASCE paper through institutional access or interlibrary loan before writing anything into S064; the existing S064 composition should be treated as unsourced until then.

results.name: TJ-2
results.notes:
COULD NOT OBTAIN AN ACCEPTABLE SOURCE, and I found no evidence that any source publishes a TJ-2 composition at all. No number is reported here.

SOURCES ATTEMPTED: the same set as S064 (ASCE JAE 2012 DOI 10.1061/(ASCE)AS.1943-5525.0000129 — Cloudflare 403, OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar both 'closed'; ASCE Earth and Space 2010 DOI 10.1061/41096(366)347 — closed, zero OA locations; the Chinese primary 蒋明镜/李立青, 岩土工程学报 2011, 33(2):209-214 at pubs.cstam.org.cn — abstract-only record, 图(0) 表(0), PDF endpoint returns HTTP 200 with a zero-byte body; cgejournal.com mirror times out; ResearchGate 403). Targeted searches for a TJ-2-specific paper, datasheet or characterisation report returned nothing — every 'TJ-2' hit resolves back to the TJ-1 literature. No local file in /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Spring - Forest on the moon/DIRT/Sources mentions TJ or Tongji.

THE DB CITATION IS CONFIRMED WRONG. R148 is 'Properties of novel LX lunar regolith simulant system — The base simulants: Part 1', Acta Astronautica, DOI 10.1016/j.actaastro.2025.02.030. That paper concerns the LX simulant family and has no connection to Tongji University's TJ series. The suspicion flagged in the task brief is correct: this citation cannot support any TJ-2 value.

INTERNAL RED FLAGS IN THE CURRENT ROW (these need no external source to establish, and are the strongest evidence of fabrication in my group):
- The S122 oxide list is item-for-item identical to S064/TJ-1 (SiO2 47.7, TiO2 2.29, Al2O3 16.2, FeO 10.75, MgO 5.04, CaO 8.21, Na2O 2.0, K2O 4.92, P2O5 0.58, MnO 0.15), i.e. TJ-1's numbers were copied onto a different product variant.
- An extra Fe2O3 = 8.3 wt% has been appended on top of an already-complete list that also carries FeO 10.75, giving oxide_sum = 106.14 wt%. A bulk oxide analysis summing to over 100% is arithmetically impossible; this value is not a transcription error but an invention.
- S122 lists specific_gravity 2.7 while S064/TJ-1 lists 2.9. The only description of TJ-2 I could find anywhere (one sentence on the secondary aggregator simulantdb.com/simulants/tj.php: 'TJ-2 was a variant spiked with silicon carbide to raise the specific gravity to 2.90') attributes the 2.90 figure to TJ-2, not TJ-1 — so the two rows may additionally have their specific gravities swapped. I could not verify this and am not asserting it.

I list no db_discrepancies because there is no acceptable source to compare against; the defects above are internal-consistency failures, not source disagreements.

RECOMMENDATION: S122's composition and its R148 citation should both be removed rather than corrected. TJ-2 is described only as a silicon-carbide-spiked density variant of TJ-1; even if the TJ-1 oxide table is later recovered from the 2012 ASCE paper, it must NOT be transferred to S122 — adding SiC changes the bulk chemistry, and no source states a composition for that exact variant. If the ASCE 2012 or Earth and Space 2010 paper turns out to publish nothing for TJ-2, the correct final verdict for this row becomes SOURCE_HAS_NO_COMPOSITION.

physical.particle_size_distribution: db '4.84-432.27 µm' | source: this range is stated for the CE-5 LUNAR SAMPLES, not the simulant - '95% (by weight) of particles of CE-5 samples ranged from 4.84 and 432.27 lm, with a median particle size of 52.54 lm [12]' (Section 2.3).
