NOT A DISCREPANCY (verified correct): all seven mineral percentages (Pyroxene 41.7, Plagioclase 32.4, Olivine 9.1, Ilmenite 6.2, Glass 5.0, Quartz 2.1, Hematite 3.4) and mineral_sum 99.9 match Section 3.2 exactly; specific_gravity 3.17 matches Table 6; particle_size_d50 40.4 matches the stated 40.40 µm; feedstock list (Basalt, Hedenbergite, Anorthite, Forsterite, Ilmenite, China tektite) matches Table 3; the R078/R103 reference DOI 10.1016/j.ijmst.2024.08.006 is the correct, real paper.
results.notes:
SOURCING. No manufacturer or technical data sheet exists for PolyU-1: it is a research-laboratory simulant (the database itself records availability as 'Unavailable') and a targeted search returned only the journal article and repository copies. The primary characterisation paper is therefore the highest-quality source available, and I obtained the publisher PDF (open access, CC BY-NC-ND) from the PolyU Institutional Research Archive after confirming open-access status via OpenAlex. ScienceDirect served only a bot-wall SPA shell and DOAJ carried no direct PDF. The saved PDF is 2,507,231 bytes, 10 pages, and its text was extracted with pdftotext -layout; page 6 (journal p.1322) was additionally rendered at 220 dpi with pdftoppm and read as an image to inspect Fig. 5 and Fig. 6.

CENTRAL FINDING. The database's oxide block for PolyU-1 is a misattribution, not a transcription error. All ten values reproduce the 'CE-5' row of Table 2, which the paper's own caption identifies as 'The average contents (%) of major elements in CE-5 lunar samples'. Those are the design TARGETS the simulant was built to approximate, measured on returned lunar material - they are not measurements of PolyU-1. The paper's Section 3.2 makes the mismatch explicit: the simulant's Na and K contents are stated to be 'obviously higher than the target values' (by 1.15% and 1.02%), so the target values 0.53 and 0.08 demonstrably are not the simulant's own. The oxide_sum 99.22 confirms the provenance arithmetically - it is precisely the sum of that CE-5 row.

I have therefore returned an EMPTY oxides array. This is deliberate and is the correct answer under the grounding rule: the paper publishes no numeric oxide wt% for the PolyU-1 simulant anywhere. Its only presentation of the simulant's chemical composition is Fig. 6, a box-and-line plot with a 'Contents (wt%)' y-axis and no printed data labels on the simulant curve, supplemented in prose only by differences from the CE-5 targets. I did not read values off the plot axes, and I did not carry the CE-5 target numbers across, because neither would be a number the source actually states for this material. Note also that Fig. 6 labels the iron axis 'FeOx', and Section 2.4 warns that 'the XRF analysis cannot distinguish between different valence states of the Fe in minerals' - so even the database's 'FeO' species label for the simulant is unsupported.

RECOMMENDATION FOR THE RECORD. The oxide block should be deleted rather than corrected; there is no published replacement. If the dashboard needs to show a chemical target for PolyU-1, it must be labelled explicitly as the Chang'e-5 lunar sample average (Table 2 of Zou et al. 2024), attributed to the lunar samples and not to the simulant.

MINERALS ARE SOUND. All seven mineral percentages in the database match Section 3.2 of the paper exactly and sum to 99.9 as recorded. Only the empty 'Anorthite: null' row is spurious - the paper treats anorthite as the form plagioclase takes, not as a separate phase. The paper also resolves pyroxene into hedenbergite 27.6% and augite 14.1%, which the database does not carry.

TWO FABRICATED PHYSICAL VALUES. The stored cohesion (6.75 kPa) and friction angle (38.0 degrees) are both exact arithmetic midpoints of the paper's published ranges (0-13.5 kPa and 35.7-40.3 degrees). Neither number appears in the paper. These are collapsed ranges presented as point measurements, and they are misleading in opposite directions: the cohesion range includes zero, and the paper's own single-number angle for the simulant is the angle of repose (38.9 degrees), a different physical quantity. The stored particle size range '4.84-432.27 um' is likewise lifted from the CE-5 lunar samples, the same misattribution pattern as the oxides. I have reported the source ranges verbatim in the physical block rather than any midpoint.

I did not modify lrs.sqlite or anything under lrs-dashboard/public or lrs-dashboard/src. The only file written outside the scratchpad is the downloaded source PDF at the reported local_copy_path. A stray 404 HTML file briefly written to that papers directory (from a first, incorrect bitstream URL supplied by a page summary) was deleted before the correct PDF was fetched.

NO COMPOSITION SOURCE OBTAINED. Every statement below comes from a document or API response I opened in this session.

1) The primary source exists but is closed access. Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1016/j.pss.2017.04.010) returned: title 'Developing a new controllable lunar dust simulant: BHLD20', Planetary and Space Science, vol 141, pp 17-24, published 2017-07, authors Hao Sun, Min Yi, Zhigang Shen, Xiaojing Zhang, Shulin Ma. Unpaywall returned is_oa=false, oa_status='closed', has_repository_copy=false, oa_locations=[] (affiliations: Beihang University / Beijing Key Lab for Powder Technology; Min Yi at TU Darmstadt). OpenAlex returned is_oa=false, only location doi.org, no pdf_url, no abstract. Semantic Scholar returned isOpenAccess=false, openAccessPdf status 'CLOSED'. The ScienceDirect article page returns HTTP 403 to WebFetch and only a bot-challenge shell to curl (1.2 MB with zero occurrences of 'BHLD'). No copy found via Google Scholar versions, ResearchGate, CORE or CNKI. Elsevier text-mining API requires a key. I therefore never read the paper's composition tables and report no numbers from it.

2) The database's cited reference contains no composition for BHLD20. I downloaded and read the full text of Duri, Caporale, Rouphael, Vingiani, Palladino, De Pascale, Adamo (2022), Front. Astron. Space Sci. 8:747821 (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/astronomy-and-space-sciences/articles/10.3389/fspas.2021.747821/pdf), archived at /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Spring - Forest on the moon/DIRT/Sources/papers/Duri_etal_2022_Regolith_Simulants_Plant_Growth_Review_FrontAstronSpaceSci_8_747821.pdf. The string 'BHLD' occurs exactly twice in the whole paper: the Table 1 row quoted above (which states only market availability and that bulk chemistry came from XRF and mineralogy from XRD/SEM, citing Sun et al. 2017) and the reference-list entry. I also rendered page 6 as an image to check Figure 2: it is four category-average pie charts (Lunar Mare, Lunar Highlands, Lunar Dust, Martian), not per-simulant values, so it gives no BHLD20 numbers either. Conclusion: the two mineral rows currently in the database (Plagioclase 25.0 %, Volcanic Glass 20.0 %, mineral_sum 45.0, no oxides) cannot have come from the only reference the database cites, and I could not trace them to any document. They should be treated as unsourced until Sun et al. 2017 is obtained. db_discrepancies is left empty because with no source in hand there is nothing to compare against - this is 'unverified', not 'verified wrong'.

3) Related document I did open, deliberately NOT used for values: the group's Chinese follow-up paper Sun Hao, Gao Haiyang, Shen Zhigang, Zhang Xiaojing, Yang Yanjing, 'Mo ni yue chen BHLD20 gai jin yan jiu' (Improvement study of lunar dust simulant BHLD20), Manned Spaceflight (Zairen Hangtian) 2018, issue 5. Its official abstract on the China Manned Space site (https://www.cmse.gov.cn/dmt/cbw/zrht/2018n/2018ndwq/201810/t20181022_40825.html) states a median particle size of 285 nm and says the main chemical composition is close to most Apollo dust samples, but gives no oxide or mineral numbers. I did not enter 285 nm as a physical property because (a) it is an abstract, not the characterisation tables, and (b) it describes the improved variant of that 2018 paper, not necessarily the 2017 PSS BHLD20 the database entry refers to. Full text is behind CNKI / an app login (the fx361 mirror is behind Cloudflare and shows only the introduction).

4) Also checked: none of the 23 PDFs already in /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Spring - Forest on the moon/DIRT/Sources/papers (including the NASA Lunar Regolith Simulant User's Guide 2010 and 2024 Rev A, and the JHUAPL/LSIC 2020 simulant assessment) contains the string 'BHLD'.

Recommendation: acquire Planet. Space Sci. 141, 17-24 (2017) through institutional access or an author request, then re-audit. Until then S005 should publish no composition at all rather than the current two unsourced mineral rows. No files were modified other than adding the archived Duri PDF to Sources/papers.

physical.friction_angle — DB: 46.2; Source: not stated. Part 1 reports no friction angle, angle of repose, shear strength or cohesion for LX-M100; the strings 'friction angle' and 'cohesion' do not occur anywhere in the paper (the only 'friction' hit is the ranked property name 'Coefficient of friction' in Table 1, a workshop priority list, not a measurement). physical.particle_size_distribution — DB: '<45-2000 µm'; Source: no particle-size range is stated for the product. The paper states 'The base simulants thus have a as mixed median particle size of 70 μm' and (Section 2.2.3) lists the fractions the simulants were separated into for morphology work: '<45 μm, 45–71 μm, 71–90 μm, 90–125 μm, 125–160 μm, 160–250 μm, 250–500 μm, 500–1000 μm and 1000–2000 μm'.

results.notes:
Source obtained locally, not downloaded: the file at /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Spring - Forest on the moon/DIRT/Properties of novel LX lunar regolith simulant system.pdf is the full Elsevier open-access PDF of Part 1 (title, authors, TU Berlin affiliations, DOI 10.1016/j.actaastro.2025.02.030 and page range 200-222 all verified inside the document). This is the primary characterisation paper that introduces LX-M100; no manufacturer datasheet exists for it as far as this session could establish. Nothing was written to the dashboard, lrs.sqlite, public/ or src/.

All numbers above were read from pdftotext -layout output AND independently confirmed by rendering pages 207 and 208 as PNGs (pdftoppm -f 8 -l 9) and reading the images, because Tables 2/3/4 are multi-column and column mis-assignment was the main risk. The rendered pages matched the text extraction exactly.

Oxides: all 11 oxide values in the DB match Table 4's LX-M100 column exactly. The DB simply omits the last two rows (LOI 0.74, Sum 100.14). Note the paper's own caveats, which the DB does not carry: FeO is not measured — footnote a states 'FeO calculated from measured Fe2O3 using a conversion factor of 0.8998' — and footnote b states 'Sum calculated using measured Fe2O3 content', so the 100.14 sum is on an Fe2O3 basis and does not equal the sum of the FeO-basis rows. Appendix Table A.13 gives the underlying triplicate XRF with all detected oxides for LX-M100 (mean Fe2O3 11.37, plus SO3 0.01, V2O5 0.02, NiO 0.04, CuO 0.02, ZnO 0.01, SrO 0.07, ZrO2 0.03, BaO 0.09, HfO2 0.11, PbO 0.00); Table 4 is the paper's own headline table and is the correct comparison for the DB's field set.

Minerals: the DB's seven phases match Table 3 exactly, but two phases the paper reports for the mixed LX-M100 simulant are missing (Chlorite 2, Biotite 1). Values are XRD, 'rounded to whole percentage'.

Physical: bulk_density 1.33 and density_g_cm3 2.86 match Table 10 (ρb 1.33 ± 0.02 g/cm3, solid/grain density ρs 2.86 ± 0.01 g/cm3); I have put ρs in the specific_gravity field because the schema has no grain-density slot — the source's own term is 'solid density ρs' in g/cm3, not specific gravity. particle_size_d50 63.7 matches Table 8 but only for the dry-sieving method; the same table gives 35.6 (wet sieving), 192.3 ± 9.2 (laser scattering) and 536.6 ± 39.6 (dynamic image analysis) for LX-M100, so the DB's bare '63.7' is method-dependent and should be labelled. The paper also reports ρmin 1.13 ± 0.04 and ρmax 1.93 ± 0.01 g/cm3, which the DB does not hold.

The friction_angle of 46.2 is the one value that is not merely incomplete but unsupported: it appears nowhere in Part 1, and the same number is stored for both S040 and S041, which is a hallmark of the fabricated-data problem that took the site offline. I did not substitute a value from memory or from Part 2 (doi 10.1016/j.actaastro.2025.01.056), which was not available locally and in any case covers the physically adapted simulants, a different product variant. Recommend the field be cleared unless a geomechanical source specific to LX-M100 is produced.

[Section 3.1.1] The XRD results shown in Table 2 confirm that the rock used as a base material for the production of LX-T100 is indeed an anorthosite. LX-T100 has a plagioclase content of around 93 wt.-%, whereby the finer fractions have a higher bytownite content than the coarser ones. Furthermore, quartz is found in the analysed size fractions and the mixed simulant in small proportions of 3 to 4 wt.-%.

minerals: Biotite — DB: 2.0 %; Source (Table 2, LX-T100 column): '<1' wt.-% (an upper bound, not a measured 1). The DB value 2 is the figure printed in the 'LX-T 1–2 mm' size-fraction column of the same table, i.e. transferred from a size fraction to the mixed simulant.
minerals: Illite — DB: absent from minerals_in_db; Source (Table 2, LX-T100 column): 2 wt.-%

physical.friction_angle — DB: 46.2; Source: not stated. Part 1 reports no friction angle, angle of repose, shear strength or cohesion for LX-T100; the strings 'friction angle' and 'cohesion' do not occur anywhere in the paper. The DB carries the identical 46.2 for both LX-T100 and LX-M100, which no source read here supports.

physical.particle_size_distribution — DB: '<45-2000 µm'; Source: no particle-size range is stated for the product. The paper states 'The base simulants thus have a as mixed median particle size of 70 μm' and (Section 2.2.3) lists the fractions the simulants were separated into for morphology work: '<45 μm, 45–71 μm, 71–90 μm, 90–125 μm, 125–160 μm, 160–250 μm, 250–500 μm, 500–1000 μm and 1000–2000 μm'.

oxide_sum (computed) — DB: 99.76; Source: this is the DB's own sum of its eleven oxide rows excluding LOI and Sum. It is arithmetically consistent with the DB rows, but because the DB's LOI is wrong (0.66 vs 0.60) any total that includes LOI will be 0.06 high. The source's stated Sum is 100.05 on an Fe2O3 basis (Table 4 footnote b), which the DB does store correctly as an oxide row named 'Sum'.
results.notes:
Source obtained locally, not downloaded: the file at /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Spring - Forest on the moon/DIRT/Properties of novel LX lunar regolith simulant system.pdf is the full Elsevier open-access PDF of Part 1 (title, authors, TU Berlin affiliations, DOI 10.1016/j.actaastro.2025.02.030 and page range 200-222 all verified inside the document). This is the primary characterisation paper that introduces LX-T100; no manufacturer datasheet exists for it as far as this session could establish. Nothing was written to the dashboard, lrs.sqlite, public/ or src/.

All numbers above were read from pdftotext -layout output AND independently confirmed by rendering pages 207 and 208 as PNGs (pdftoppm -f 8 -l 9) and reading the images, because Tables 2/3/4 are multi-column and column mis-assignment was the main risk. The rendered pages matched the text extraction exactly. That visual check is what pins down the two column-transfer errors below.

IMPORTANT on the Biotite entry in my minerals array: the source prints '<1' for LX-T100 Biotite, i.e. an upper bound, not the number 1. The output schema requires a numeric pct, so I entered 1 as the nearest faithful placeholder. The source does NOT state 1; it states '<1'. A reviewer should record it as '<1 wt.-%' rather than a point value. Because of this, the paper's LX-T100 mineral column sums to slightly under 100 (40+53+3+<1+2+2), consistent with the text's statement that 'LX-T100 has a plagioclase content of around 93 wt.-%' (bytownite 40 + labradorite 53).

Two of the four substantive errors here are column transfers within Table 4 / Table 2 — LOI taken from the LX-M 1–2 mm column, Biotite taken from the LX-T 1–2 mm fraction column — which is exactly the failure mode the task warns about (never transfer numbers between variants or sieve fractions). Illite 2 wt.-% is simply missing.

Eleven of the thirteen oxide entries match Table 4's LX-T100 column exactly, including the stated Sum of 100.05. Note the paper's caveats that the DB does not carry: FeO is not measured — footnote a states 'FeO calculated from measured Fe2O3 using a conversion factor of 0.8998' — and footnote b states 'Sum calculated using measured Fe2O3 content', so 100.05 is on an Fe2O3 basis and is not the sum of the FeO-basis rows. Appendix Table A.12 gives the underlying triplicate XRF for LX-T100 with all detected oxides (mean Fe2O3 0.63, plus SO3 0.02, NiO 0.05, CuO 0.04, HfO2 0.10, etc.).

Physical: bulk_density 1.35 and density_g_cm3 2.73 match Table 10 (ρb 1.35 ± 0.01 g/cm3, solid/grain density ρs 2.73 ± 0.00 g/cm3); ρs is reported in the specific_gravity field only because the schema has no grain-density slot — the source's own term is 'solid density ρs' in g/cm3. particle_size_d50 73.5 matches Table 8 but only for dry sieving; the same table gives 66.6 (wet sieving), 142.3 ± 11.0 (laser scattering) and 393.4 ± 38.4 (dynamic image analysis) for LX-T100, so the bare '73.5' is method-dependent and should be labelled. The paper also reports ρmin 1.17 ± 0.02 and ρmax 1.93 ± 0.01 g/cm3, which the DB does not hold.

As with S040, the friction_angle of 46.2 is unsupported by anything I opened and is identical across both simulants. I did not substitute a value from memory or from Part 2 (doi 10.1016/j.actaastro.2025.01.056), which is not present anywhere on the drive and in any case covers the physically adapted simulants, a different product variant. Recommend the field be cleared unless a geomechanical source specific to LX-T100 is produced.

[Section 3.2.1, p.5] "TUBS-M basalt is part of an alkali-olivine basalt occurrence in Germany. Hand specimens are fine grained and dense without degassing vesicles. Microphenocrysts are rather rare (<5 vol%) and predominantly olivine followed by rare clinopyroxene (augite; Fig. 6). The densely packed clinopyroxene - plagioclase (labradorite with An50) matrix appears in thin section without major alteration. ... Titanomagnetite makes <3 vol% of the total mineral content. Accessory (<<1 vol%) interstitial mineral phases are anorthoclase feldspar ... iron oxides and zeolite"
db_discrepancies: oxides / P2O5: db value = absent (oxide not in db); source value = 0.51 wt% (Linke et al. 2020, Table 2, TUBS-M analysis column)
oxides / LOI: db value = absent (not in db); source value = 0.63 wt% (Table 2)
oxide_sum: db value = 96.96; source value = 98.09 (Table 2 'Sum' row for TUBS-M). The 1.13 difference is exactly the omitted P2O5 (0.51) + LOI (0.63) minus rounding.

physical.particle_size_d50: db value = 76.7 (um); source value = 87 um ('Median 87 um', Table 5). The db number 76.7 is not in this paper; it is the x50 of TUBS-M in Windisch et al. 2022 (Materials 15, 8561, Table 2), a different paper than the one the db cites (R054).

physical.particle_size_distribution: db value = 'x_50 = 76.7 to 96.0 um'; source value = 'Particle size range 0-2.0 mm; Median 87 um' (Table 5). The db string is not a range for TUBS-M at all: 76.7 um is TUBS-M's x50 and 96.0 um is TUBS-T's x50 in Windisch et al. 2022 Table 2, i.e. two different simulants' values fused into one fake range.

physical.cohesion: db value = 0.35 (kPa); source value = 0.6 kPa (Table 5). The db number corresponds to 349.67 Pa, the TUBS-M cohesion at 3 kPa shear stress in Windisch et al. 2022 Table A3 (a single test point, not the paper's headline value).

physical (missing fields): db holds none of the following that the source states for TUBS-M: tapped density 1.81 g/cm3, Hausner ratio 1.28, angle of repose 41.9-45.8 deg, average aspect ratio 0.634, particle size range 0-2.0 mm.
results.notes: Composition: the db's ten oxides for TUBS-M reproduce Linke et al. 2020 Table 2 exactly, digit for digit; the chemistry is correct as far as it goes but is truncated (P2O5 and LOI dropped), which is why the db's oxide_sum (96.96) does not match the paper's published Sum (98.09). Minerals: the paper publishes no modal mineral table for TUBS-M - only qualitative/limit statements (microphenocrysts <5 vol% predominantly olivine, titanomagnetite <3 vol%, accessory phases <<1 vol%, matrix of clinopyroxene + plagioclase labradorite An50). I therefore report no mineral percentages; the db's empty mineral list is not wrong, and any numeric modal composition for TUBS-M would have to come from elsewhere. Table 4 of the paper gives mineral-by-mineral element chemistry (olivine, plagioclase, clinopyroxene, Fe-Ti-spinel) but NOT modal abundances - it must not be read as a mineral composition. Physical: the paper's own Table 5 values are reported above; I verified them on a rendered image of page 8 because pdftotext drops the +/- and degree symbols. Angle of repose for TUBS-T reads 37.91 deg (single value) in the rendered page, confirmed. Source hunt: no manufacturer/technical datasheet for TUBS-M is publicly obtainable - the paper itself only promises that 'data sheets ... will be completed' in early 2020, and web searches return only journal articles, so the primary characterisation paper is the best available source. Note also that the repo's documentation/paper-simulant-index.md attributes TUBS-M composition to 'Toklu et al. 2023 - Production of a set of lunar regolith simulants based on Apollo and Chinese samples'; that paper is real (Adv. Space Res. 72, 565-576) but it concerns the Turkish simulant TBG-1 and Chang'e-5 analogues, not TUBS - that index entry is a mis-attribution and should not be used as a TUBS source. Secondary cross-check read in this session: Windisch et al. 2022, 'Geotechnical and Shear Behavior of Novel Lunar Regolith Simulants TUBS-M, TUBS-T, and TUBS-I', Materials 15(23) 8561, doi:10.3390/ma15238561, full text XML read from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC9737658/fullTextXML. That paper publishes NO composition of its own (it refers back to Linke et al. 2020), but its Table 2 gives x50 = 76.7 um (TUBS-M) and 96.0 um (TUBS-T) and bulk density 1.41-1.62 (TUBS-M) / 1.33-1.46 g/cm3 (TUBS-T), and Table A3 gives cohesion 349.67 Pa (TUBS-M) / 642.67 Pa (TUBS-T) at 3 kPa. So the db's physical numbers are traceable to a real second primary paper - they are not fabricated - but they are filed under the wrong citation and stripped of their measurement conditions and ranges.

results.notes:
SOURCE HUNT. The primary characterisation paper (Battler M.M. & Spray J.G. 2009, Planet. Space Sci. 57, 2128-2131, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2009.09.003) could NOT be obtained: ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403, and Unpaywall reports is_oa=false with zero OA locations (Crossref confirmed title/authors/pages). Battler's 2008 UNB M.Sc. thesis is listed as unpublished and I found no downloadable copy. No Deltion/NORCAT manufacturer datasheet for OB-1 is published anywhere I could reach. I therefore report NOTHING from the primary paper, and fell back to the best agency report.

WHAT THE DB GETS RIGHT. All eight oxide values in the db for S053 match Slabic 2024 Table 7 row 'OB-1(A*)' exactly (49.7 / 1.5 / 16.8 / 11.8 / 5.8 / 9.7 / 2.5 / 0.7; sum 98.5 = db oxide_sum 98.5). That row is XRF data measured by Steve Wilson (USGS, 2020) on OB-1 itself, so the db chemistry for OB-1 is genuinely sourced and correct. physical.glass_content_percent = 42.0 is also supported: Slabic states OB-1 is '42% glass, 58% anorthosite', and the NASA ARES page says '58% Shawmere Anorthosite ... and 42% fayalitic olivine slag glass'. Note this is the formulation ratio, not the measured modal glass (45.5 % per Slabic Table 5; 52.6 % per Schrader et al. 2010).

WHAT IS FABRICATED. The mineral list is not reproducible from any source. Six of the ten db phases (Magnetite, Quartz, Smectite, Saponite, Undifferentiated, Plagioclase Glass) appear in no OB-1 dataset I opened. Smectite and saponite are hydrous clays and are geologically impossible in this material; they look transplanted from a Mars simulant. The list also sums to 102.04 %, which no modal analysis reports.

CROSS-CHECKS I ACTUALLY OPENED (not used as the reported numbers, but they bound the answer):
1) Schrader, C.M., Rickman, D.L., McLemore, C.A., Fikes, J.C. (2010) NASA/TM-2010-216446, Table 2 (local file .../Schrader_etal_2010_Lunar_Regolith_Simulant_Users_Guide_NASA-TM-2010-216446.pdf), QEMSCAN SEM/EDS particle-type modal data for OB-1: Glass 52.6, Plagioclase 43.9 (Plag. An% 75), Olivine 0.0, Clinopyroxene 0.1, Spinel minerals 0.19, Ilmenite 0.0, Other (sim. only) 3.1, Total 100. The same report notes the area-modal data show mafic minerals in OB-1 only because 'pixels in the OB-1 olivine slag glass [are] being reported as mafic phases'. Table 3 gives OB-1 a FoM composition score of 0.28 against lunar reference 64001/64002. This report contains no oxide chemistry for OB-1.
2) NASA ARES OB-1 page, https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/projects/simulants/ob-1.html (downloaded to /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Spring - Forest on the moon/DIRT/Sources/papers/NASA_ARES_OB-1_page.html). Its 'Major Element Chemistry' table has an OB-1 column that is entirely dashes - ARES publishes NO OB-1 oxide chemistry; the oxide numbers on that page (SiO2 48.28, Al2O3 32.01, FeO 1.34, Fe2O3 0.09, MgO 0.22, CaO 15.43, Na2O 2.38, K2O 0.16, TiO2 0.05, P2O5 0.01, MnO 0.01, LOI+H2O 0.39) are for the Shawmere Anorthosite FEEDSTOCK, cited to Battler & Spray 2009 - they must not be used as OB-1's composition. ARES physical properties for OB-1: Specific Gravity 3.071 g/cm3, Bulk Density 1.815 g/cm3, Mean Particle Size 82.25 um; cohesion, friction angle, Young's modulus and tensile strength are all blank. ARES also carries a second OB-1 modal column (cited to a 2008 Schrader PTMSS presentation): Glass 43.22, Quartz 0.48, Plagioclase 44.35, Orthoclase 0.08, Olivine 6.27, Clinopyroxene 2.95, Orthopyroxene 0.19, Sulphides 0.35, Ilmenite 0.00, Magnetite 0.07, MgFeAl silicate 1.83, Native iron 0.01, Chromite 0.01, Calcite 0.08, Other 0.12, Total 100.00.
3) Denevi et al. 2020 JHU-APL Lunar Simulant Assessment and Stockstill-Cahill et al. 2021 JHU-APL Lunar Simulant Assessment: both opened; neither contains any OB-1 measurement, only a bibliographic citation to Battler & Spray 2009.

CAUTION FOR THE REBUILD: the Slabic 2024 row is labelled 'OB-1(A*)' and its Table 5 mineralogy (Glass 45.5 / Pyroxene 2.6 / Plagioclase Feldspar 46.2 / Olivine 5.6) does not reconcile with Schrader et al. 2010 Table 2 for OB-1 (Glass 52.6 / Plagioclase 43.9 / Olivine 0.0 / Clinopyroxene 0.1). These are two genuinely different published datasets for the same material; whichever you adopt should be attributed explicitly, and they should not be blended.

db_discrepancies: oxides / SiO2: db 48.3 wt% vs source 49.7 wt% (Slabic 2024 Table 7, row OB-1(A*)). 48.3 appears in no source I opened.

Five of the eight db oxides (TiO2 1.5, FeO 11.8, MgO 5.8, Na2O 2.5, K2O 0.7) are copied verbatim from that OB-1 row while three were altered, which is not a pattern any single measurement can produce.

mineral_sum: db 97.3 vs source 99.9 - the 2.6 shortfall is exactly the dropped pyroxene.

physical / specific_gravity: db 1.51 vs source: no specific gravity is published for OB-1A (or any simulant) in this document. 1.51 is the OB-1A rho(min) BULK DENSITY in g/cm3 from Table 16, mislabelled as specific gravity. The db value is also self-inconsistent - a specific gravity of 1.51 is lower than the db's own bulk density of 1.57, which is physically impossible, and true anorthosite specific gravity is near 2.7-3.1 (NASA ARES lists 3.071 for OB-1).
physical / bulk_density: db 1.57 vs source 1.51 (rho_min) and 1.63 (rho_max) g/cm3 for OB-1A. 1.57 appears nowhere for OB-1A; it is the JSC-1A rho(min) value in the same Table 16 row block.
minerals / provenance: the source states 'no direct mineralogical measurement of OB-1A exists' - the db's mineral list should not be presented as measured on OB-1A.
results.notes:
SOURCE HUNT. No manufacturer datasheet for OB-1A from Deltion Innovations exists on the open web that I could reach, and there is no primary characterisation paper for OB-1A (Battler & Spray 2009 covers OB-1 only, and is in any case paywalled - ScienceDirect HTTP 403, Unpaywall is_oa=false, no OA locations). The NASA ARES simulant page at https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/projects/simulants/ob-1.html covers OB-1 and CHENOBI and never mentions OB-1A. The JHU-APL 2021 Lunar Simulant Assessment (which I downloaded and searched in full) contains no OB-1A data; the geotechnical numbers are attributed to 'APL SAR 2022', a report I could not locate publicly. Slabic et al. 2024 Rev A is therefore the best obtainable source, and it is the appropriate one - it is the current NASA user's guide and is the document that actually defines OB-1A.

THE CENTRAL FINDING. Slabic 2024 states twice, explicitly, that NO direct chemistry and NO direct mineralogy measurement of OB-1A exists - both are OB-1 measurements extrapolated to OB-1A because the feedstocks are similar. Every composition number in the db for S054 is therefore, at best, OB-1 data wearing an OB-1A label, and it should be flagged as extrapolated rather than measured. I have reported the source's OB-1(A*) values above because they are the only published figures, but a reviewer should note the provenance caveat is part of the source's own text.

WHAT THE DB GETS RIGHT. Four physical values are correctly sourced: particle_size_d50 138.5 (= Table 10 Q50 for OB-1A, laser diffraction, Clark 2021 JSC-ARES), cohesion 15.0 kPa and friction_angle 35.0 deg (= Table 19 averages, APL SAR 2022 direct shear), and glass_content_percent 40.0 (= 'consisted of 60% Shawmere anorthosite, and 40% glass slag'). Note d50 138.5 is a Q50 quartile from laser diffraction, not a sieve d50, so the field name is loose but the number is real.

WHAT IS WRONG. Three of the eight oxides (SiO2 48.3, Al2O3 16.3, CaO 11.0) disagree with the only published figures and match nothing I read, while the other five are copied verbatim from the same row - a signature of hand-edited rather than measured data. The mineral list silently drops Pyroxene 2.6 %. And the two density fields are the clearest error: 1.51 is OB-1A's minimum bulk density in g/cm3 relabelled as specific gravity, and 1.57 belongs to JSC-1A in the same table. The resulting db record claims a specific gravity below its own bulk density.

ADDITIONAL SOURCED DATA THE DB IS MISSING (all from the same document, all specific to OB-1A): rho_max 1.63 g/cm3 and rho_min 1.51 g/cm3 (Table 16); PSD Q25 68.1 um and Q75 417.8 um (Table 10); particle geometry AR 0.59 and root form factor 0.89 (Table 13); magnetic susceptibility log(chi) 3.22 (Table 22); and the FoM scores listed in the physical block above. Also worth recording: the document's summary table gives OB-1A a Chemistry FoM of 'n/a' while its Table 8 lists OB-1(A*) chemistry FoM = 87 - an internal inconsistency in the source itself, presumably because the chemistry is extrapolated.

REFERENCES CURRENTLY ON THE DB RECORD. R060 (Slabic et al. 2024) is the correct source and is already cited, but only as type 'usage' - it is in fact the composition and geotechnical source and should be retyped. R092 (NASA ARES OB-1 page) is cited as 'composition,geotechnical' for S054, but that page is about OB-1, never mentions OB-1A, and publishes no oxide chemistry for either - it cannot support the db's S054 composition and should be removed or re-scoped.

oxides.Al2O3: db 16.7 wt%, source (Table 3, 'Bag All') 17 wt%. 16.7 is again the Table 1 W172158 source-rock value.
oxides.MgO: db 6.5 wt%, source (Table 3, 'Bag All') 8 wt%. 6.5 is the Table 1 W172158 source-rock value.
oxides.CaO: db 9.2 wt%, source (Table 3, 'Bag All') 14 wt%. 9.2 is the Table 1 W172158 source-rock value; the TM explicitly notes the higher Ca in BP-1 is real and due to secondary minerals.
oxides.Na2O: db 2.3 wt%, source (Table 3, 'Bag All') 3 wt%. Table 1 W172158 Na2O is 3.5, not 2.3 - the db value 2.3 is actually W172158's TiO2 figure placed in the Na2O row.
oxides.K2O: db 3.5 wt%, source (Table 3, 'Bag All') 0 wt%. Table 1 W172158 K2O is 1.1, not 3.5 - the db value 3.5 is actually W172158's Na2O figure placed in the K2O row.

oxides.TiO2: db 1.1 wt%, source reports no TiO2 for BP-1 in Table 3; Table 1 W172158 TiO2 is 2.3 wt%. The db value 1.1 is actually W172158's K2O figure placed in the TiO2 row. (The TM text states the Black Point basalt TiO2 content is 2.2-2.3%.)
oxides.FeO: db 5.9 wt%, source Table 3 'Bag All' reports Fe2O3 11 wt% and no FeO at all; Table 1 W172158 gives FeO 6.2 and Fe2O3 5.9. The db has entered the Fe2O3 number under the label FeO.
oxides.P2O5: db 0.52 wt%, source reports no P2O5 for BP-1 in Table 3; 0.52 is the Table 1 W172158 source-rock value.
oxides.MnO: db 0.21 wt%, source reports no MnO for BP-1 in Table 3; 0.21 is the Table 1 W172158 source-rock value.

oxide_sum: db 93.13, source Table 3 'Bag All' Total 100 (Table 1 W172158 Total 99.90). The db sum is an artefact of the mislabelled/partial oxide set.

physical.specific_gravity: db 1.43 (dimensionless). The source states no specific gravity at all. 1.43 corresponds to the RELATIVE MINIMUM DENSITY in g/cm3 tabulated on the NASA ARES BP-1 page (which cites Suescun-Florez et al. 2015); that page gives specific gravity as 2.81 g/cm3. The db field appears to hold a minimum-density value under a specific-gravity label.
results.notes:
SOURCE: The defining characterisation document for BP-1 is NASA/TM-2010-216444, 'Preliminary Geological Findings on the BP-1 Simulant', Stoeser (USGS), Rickman (MSFC) & Wilson (USGS), September 2010. Downloaded from NTRS (the exact URL already carried in db reference R082), saved locally, read with pdftotext -layout, and every table independently re-verified by rendering PDF pages 13, 14 and 15 to PNG at 130 dpi and reading the images. BP-1 is quarry washing waste from the Black Point basalt flow, not a manufactured product, so no manufacturer datasheet exists; this NASA TM is the highest-quality source available.

WHICH TABLE IS BP-1's COMPOSITION: the TM contains two different chemical tables and they are NOT interchangeable. Table 1 is a whole-rock analysis of the Black Point LAVA FLOW taken from the USGS National Geochemical Database (samples W172158 west and W172154 east) - i.e. the source rock, not the simulant. Table 3 is the XRF analysis of actual BP-1 material sampled from five 1-ton lots, with a 'Bag All' column. I report the 'Bag All' column as BP-1's oxide composition. This matches how NASA ARES itself presents it: the ARES BP-1 page (fetched this session, https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/projects/simulants/bp-1.html) labels that same column 'BP-1 avg of 5 samples wt. %' and labels the W172158/W172154 columns '*Two samples from the west and east of the flow'. Caveat the reviewer should see: the TM's own text describes Table 3 as the analysis of the '<10-um splits' of BP-1, so it is strictly a fine fraction, and the values are reported only to whole percent with no TiO2/MnO/P2O5 reported. If the database prefers to record the source-rock analysis instead, it must be labelled as such and must then use Table 1 W172158 verbatim: SiO2 47.2, Al2O3 16.7, TiO2 2.3, Fe2O3 5.9, FeO 6.2, MgO 6.5, MnO 0.21, CaO 9.2, Na2O 3.5, K2O 1.1, P2O5 0.52, H2O- 0.11, H2O+ 0.41, CO2 0.05, Total 99.90.

WHAT WENT WRONG IN THE DB: the db oxide list is Table 1 column W172158 (the source rock, mislabelled as the simulant) with three rows shuffled and one relabelled. Specifically TiO2/Na2O/K2O were rotated (source TiO2 2.3 -> db Na2O; source Na2O 3.5 -> db K2O; source K2O 1.1 -> db TiO2), and the source's Fe2O3 value 5.9 was entered under the label FeO while the real FeO 6.2 and the H2O/CO2 rows were dropped. Every one of the ten db oxide numbers is individually present somewhere in Table 1, so this is a transcription/row-alignment corruption rather than pure invention.

MINERALOGY IS CORRECT: minerals_in_db reproduces Table 4 ('XRD of bulk BP-1 simulant') exactly - Labradorite 60.7, Augite 23.7, Quartz 1.7, Magnetite 3, Calcite 2.7, Olivine 6.2, Hematite 2, summing to 100.0. No discrepancy. Note the TM itself warns these are preliminary and unverified, that plagioclase is far more abundant in this single bulk sample than in the <10-um splits of Table 5, and that calcite, quartz and possibly all the hematite are secondary weathering products.

PHYSICAL PROPERTIES - NOT VERIFIABLE FROM THIS SOURCE: NASA/TM-2010-216444 publishes NO numeric physical properties. Section 4 gives particle size only as two reproduced figures (cumulative frequency and abundance vs. size, from Rahmatian & Metzger) with no tabulated D50, no density, no specific gravity, no cohesion and no friction angle. I therefore left the physical block empty rather than guess. Consequently the db values bulk_density 1.65, specific_gravity 1.43, particle_size_d50 88.4, cohesion 1.0 and friction_angle 45.0 are all UNSOURCED by the composition reference and should be treated as unverified. For the reviewer's orientation only (secondary, do not ingest as sourced values): the NASA ARES BP-1 page I fetched this session tabulates specific gravity 2.81 g/cm3, bulk density 1.5-1.6 g/cm3, relative max density 1.86, relative min density 1.43, void ratio 0.49-0.965, cohesion 0-2.0 kPa, friction angle 39-51 deg and mean particle size 100 um, citing Suescun-Florez et al. (2015) and Rahmatian & Metzger (2010). That makes the db's specific_gravity 1.43 almost certainly the relative MINIMUM DENSITY mis-filed as specific gravity, and puts db cohesion 1.0 kPa and friction angle 45 deg as single point values invented from within published ranges rather than measured figures.

SOURCES I COULD NOT OBTAIN: Suescun-Florez, Roslyakov, Iskander & Baamer (2015), J. Aerospace Eng. 28(5) 04014124 - the primary geotechnical paper and the correct authority for the physical block - is paywalled at ASCE and I could not open a full text (ResearchGate/NTRS/institutional mirrors all failed). I did open Sibille, Mueller & Mantovani, 'Geotechnical Properties of BP-1 Lunar Regolith Simulant', 2019 Lunar ISRU Workshop presentation (https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lunarisru2019/presentations/5068_Mueller.pdf), but it is review_or_secondary: it reprints Stoeser's Table 1 and Table 4 and paraphrases Suescun-Florez, so I did not draw any reported number from it. Recommendation: acquire Suescun-Florez et al. (2015) before republishing any BP-1 physical property.

Table 1. List of major oxides (average wt.%) for White Mountain feldspar. XRF data provided by Hudson Resources.

    A CIPW Norm calculation based on the chemistry XRF data provided by Hudson Resources resulted in a plagioclase content of 94 wt. %, similar to Knudsen et al. X-ray diffraction analyses and whole pattern fitting and Rietveld refinement suggest a plagioclase content of approximately 82 wt. %. Other mineral components identified include pyroxene (~5 wt.%), quartz (~7 wt. %), and ~6 wt.% of an assemblage of minor minerals (muscovite, calcite, chamosite, and orthoclase). Laser particle size distribution analysis of the GreenSpar 250 material indicated a particle size range of 250-3 m, with a graphical mean particle size of 76 m. Thermal and evolved gas analysis resulted in only a very small amount of gases produced (~0.8 wt.% loss through heating up to 1000 °C), with CO2 being the most significant gas release (likely form the calcite present in the material).

[from the same abstract, product identification:] The GreenSpar product is available in two size ranges, GreenSpar 250 ( 250 m) and GreenSpar 90 ( 90 m). NASA Johnson Space Center's Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science (ARES) division has conducted a preliminary analysis on the GreenSpar 250 material, for possible use as a lunar highlands and polar regolith simulant component.

results.notes:
What I opened, in this session: (1) the primary source, Gruener et al. (2020) LPSC 51 abstract 2867, downloaded from hou.usra.edu and read with pdftotext -layout - this is the paper that introduced White Mountain / GreenSpar anorthosite as a lunar simulant component, and it carries the only published composition measured for the material NASA evaluated (GreenSpar 250); (2) the local copy of NASA/TM-20240011783 (Lunar Regolith Simulant User's Guide Rev A) at /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Spring - Forest on the moon/DIRT/Sources/papers/Slabic_etal_2024_Lunar_Regolith_Simulant_Users_Guide_RevA_NASA-TM-20240011783.pdf; (3) the NASA ARES GreenSpar page (https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/projects/simulants/greenspar.html), fetched as raw HTML; (4) the Hudson Resources 'Calcium Feldspar' SDS (Rev 2, 24 Sep 2019) linked from that page, saved to /Volumes/Extreme SSD/Spring - Forest on the moon/DIRT/Sources/papers/Hudson_Resources_GreenSpar_Calcium_Feldspar_SDS_Rev2_2019-09-24.pdf.

On the lead about the NASA guide: the Rev A guide DOES list GreenSpar. Table 7 (p.34) gives 'GreenSpar Highlands 51.0 0.0 30.6 0.4 0.2 14.7 2.5 0.2, Wilson USGS 2020' - the database's eight oxide values are a verbatim copy of that row, so they are not fabricated, but they are a different (USGS, Steve Wilson 2020) analysis reported under the guide's fixed eight-oxide FoM scheme, with iron forced into an FeO column. Rev A Table 5 (p.32, verified by rendering the page image because the table extracts as OCR garble) gives GreenSpar a single modal-mineralogy entry, 'Anorthosite 90', referenced to 'Hudson Resources'. Rev A also gives, for GreenSpar: PSD Q25/Q50/Q75 = 37.5 / 78.0 / 141.2 um for 'GreenSpar (250um)' (Clark, 2021, JSC-ARES); AR 0.62 and root-FF 0.90; magnetic susceptibility log(chi) 0.95; FoM scores chemistry 86, mineralogy n/a, particle size 79, particle shape 84, bulk density n/a, magnetic susceptibility 06, shear strength n/a; blank (no data) rows for min/max density and for cohesion/friction angle. I did not put any of these Rev A numbers in the oxides/minerals/physical fields above because Rev A is an agency compilation and ranks below the primary paper in the stated source order.

On the manufacturer-datasheet lead: I could not obtain a Hudson Resources / Lumina technical data sheet for the exact simulant product (GreenSpar 250 or GreenSpar 90). A 'GreenSpar Technical Data Sheet' exists on SlideShare but the page returned a 3 KB stub to me and I could not read the document itself; from the search snippet it covers grades GS-60 / GS-45 / GS-15, which are finer paint-filler grades, not GreenSpar 250, so I would not have used its numbers for this entry in any case. lumina.gl/anorthosite, /products and /applications all return 404. The Hudson Resources SDS I did open is a hazard document for generic 'Calcium Feldspar': it gives ingredient ranges (Feldspar 95-99%, crystalline silica/quartz 1-5%) and, in section 9, melting point 1300-1350 C, pH 9-10 in water suspension, specific density '2,6 g/cm3' - no oxide analysis and no PSD, so it is not a composition source.

Caveats on my transcription: pdftotext drops the micron symbol, so the source's '250-3 m' and '76 m' are '250-3 um' and '76 um'. I entered particle_size_range as '250-3' exactly as the source orders it (high to low) and left particle_size_d50 empty on purpose - the source reports a graphical MEAN of 76 um, not a median, and I will not relabel it as d50. MnO, Cr2O3 and V2O5 are reported as '< 0.01' and are therefore not in the numeric oxides array. The source's mineral percentages are all prefixed 'approximately' or '~'; I kept the qualifier in the component names. The source's oxide table is headed 'White Mountain feldspar. XRF data provided by Hudson Resources' - i.e. vendor XRF on the feedstock, reproduced in the primary paper; the mineralogy and PSD are NASA ARES measurements on GreenSpar 250 specifically.

One further cross-check worth flagging for the reviewer, not used as my source: the NASA ARES GreenSpar page carries two chemistry columns, 'GreenSpar[1]' (= the Gruener 2020 numbers I report) and a separate 'GreenSpar (Hudson Resources)' column reading SiO2 50.69, Al2O3 30.47, Fe2O3 0.44, MgO 0.31, CaO 14.64, Na2O 2.44, K2O 0.19, LOI+H2O 0.67. So at least three different analyses of this material are in circulation (Gruener/Hudson XRF, ARES's Hudson column, and Wilson USGS 2020 as tabulated in Rev A), and the database silently carries the third while citing only Rev A. The single unambiguous error is physical.specific_gravity = 0.95, which is a magnetic-susceptibility log value mislabelled as a density; every source I opened that states a specific gravity for this material says 2.6.
